subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Place value of digits in whole numbers (up to 4 digits)

source_trace: Recognise the values of digits in whole numbers to at least 4-digit numbers. Example: The place value of each digit in 4 371 is: Thousands Hundreds Tens Units 4 3 7 1
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 19, TERM 1 Grade 4, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Recognise the place value of a digit in a whole number with up to 4 digits.
Use a place value table (Thousands, Hundreds, Tens, Units) to find the value of any digit.
Explain, in your own words, why the same digit can mean different amounts depending on where it sits.

english_content.narration_script: Have you ever looked at a number like 4 371 and wondered why the '4' at the start seems so much more important than the '1' at the end? That's exactly what we're exploring today: place value. Every digit in a number has two jobs -- what it looks like, and where it sits -- and its position tells us how much it's really worth. Let's build a place value table together, with four columns: Thousands, Hundreds, Tens, and Units. Now let's place the digits of 4 371 into those columns, one at a time, starting from the left: 4 goes into Thousands, 3 goes into Hundreds, 7 goes into Tens, and 1 goes into Units. Here's the key idea: the 4 isn't just '4' -- because it's sitting in the Thousands column, it's actually worth 4 000. The 3 is worth 300, the 7 is worth 70, and the 1 is worth just 1. If we add those real values together -- 4 000 plus 300 plus 70 plus 1 -- we get 4 371 right back again. That's the whole secret of place value: a number is really just the sum of what each of its digits is worth in its own column. This matters in everyday life too -- when you read a price tag, a phone number, or a sports score, you're using place value without even noticing, because your brain has already learned to read digits by their position. As you get more comfortable with this, you'll be able to look at any 4-digit number and instantly know what each digit is really worth, which will make addition, subtraction and rounding much easier later this term. Let's practise this once more with a different number: 5 682. Placed into our table, 5 is in Thousands (worth 5 000), 6 is in Hundreds (worth 600), 8 is in Tens (worth 80), and 2 is in Units (worth 2). So the digit 6 here has a place value of Hundreds, worth 600 -- not simply 'six'. It also helps to work backwards: if you're told a number has 3 in Thousands, 0 in Hundreds, 4 in Tens, and 9 in Units, you can rebuild it column by column to get 3 049. Notice the 0 still holds its place in the Hundreds column, even though it adds no value -- leaving it out would completely change the number to 349, which is wrong. This 'rebuilding' skill -- going from place values back to a full number -- is just as important as reading a number forwards, and it's exactly the skill you'll need whenever you're asked to write a number described only by its digits' values.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: An empty place value table with four column headers: Thousands, Hundreds, Tens, Units.
The digits 4, 3, 7, 1 sliding one at a time into the four columns, each landing with a soft highlight.
Each column expanding to show its real value: 4 -> 4000, 3 -> 300, 7 -> 70, 1 -> 1.
The four expanded values collapsing back together into 4 371, with a checkmark.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Het jy al ooit na 'n getal soos 4 371 gekyk en gewonder hoekom die '4' aan die begin soveel belangriker lyk as die '1' aan die einde? Dit is presies wat ons vandag ondersoek: plekwaarde. Elke syfer in 'n getal het twee take -- hoe dit lyk, en waar dit staan -- en sy posisie vertel ons hoeveel dit werklik werd is. Kom ons bou saam 'n plekwaardetabel, met vier kolomme: Duisende, Honderde, Tiene, en Eenhede. Kom ons plaas nou die syfers van 4 371 een vir een in daardie kolomme, van links af: 4 gaan in Duisende, 3 gaan in Honderde, 7 gaan in Tiene, en 1 gaan in Eenhede. Hier is die sleutel-idee: die 4 is nie net '4' nie -- omdat dit in die Duisende-kolom sit, is dit eintlik 4 000 werd. Die 3 is 300 werd, die 7 is 70 werd, en die 1 is net 1 werd. As ons daardie werklike waardes bymekaar tel -- 4 000 plus 300 plus 70 plus 1 -- kry ons weer 4 371. Dit is die hele geheim van plekwaarde: 'n getal is eintlik net die som van wat elke syfer in sy eie kolom werd is. Dit is ook belangrik in die alledaagse lewe -- wanneer jy 'n pryskaartjie, 'n telefoonnommer, of 'n sporttelling lees, gebruik jy plekwaarde sonder om dit eers agter te kom, want jou brein het reeds geleer om syfers volgens hul posisie te lees. Namate jy hiermee gemakliker raak, sal jy na enige 4-syfergetal kan kyk en dadelik weet wat elke syfer werklik werd is, wat later vanjaar optel, aftrek en afrond baie makliker sal maak. Kom ons oefen dit weer met 'n ander getal: 5 682. In ons tabel geplaas, is 5 in Duisende (5 000 werd), 6 is in Honderde (600 werd), 8 is in Tiene (80 werd), en 2 is in Eenhede (2 werd). So die syfer 6 hier het 'n plekwaarde van Honderde, 600 werd -- nie eenvoudig 'ses' nie. Dit help ook om agteruit te werk: as jy vertel word 'n getal het 3 in Duisende, 0 in Honderde, 4 in Tiene, en 9 in Eenhede, kan jy dit kolom vir kolom herbou om 3 049 te kry. Let op die 0 hou steeds sy plek in die Honderde-kolom, al voeg dit geen waarde by nie -- om dit uit te laat sou die getal heeltemal na 349 verander, wat verkeerd is. Hierdie 'herbou'-vaardigheid -- om van plekwaardes terug na 'n volle getal te gaan -- is net so belangrik as om 'n getal vorentoe te lees, en dit is presies die vaardigheid wat jy nodig sal hê wanneer jy gevra word om 'n getal te skryf wat net deur sy syfers se waardes beskryf word.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Using a place value table to read a number

source_trace: The place value of: a) 4 is Thousands b) 3 is Hundreds c) 7 is Tens d) 1 is Units
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 19, TERM 1 Grade 4, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Use a place value table to name the place value of any digit in a 4-digit number, without guessing.
Practise reading a number digit-by-digit into its correct column.
Construct a number correctly when given the value of each of its digits (the reverse of reading one).

english_content.narration_script: In our last lesson we discovered that every digit's position gives it a real value. Today, let's turn that idea into a reliable tool you can use any time you're unsure: the place value table itself. Here's how it works, step by step. First, draw four boxes in a row, and label them, from left to right, Thousands, Hundreds, Tens, Units. Second, take your number -- let's use 4 371 again -- and write each digit into its own box, always starting from the left. Third, read the label above each box to know exactly what that digit means. Using 4 371: a) the 4 is in the Thousands box, b) the 3 is in the Hundreds box, c) the 7 is in the Tens box, and d) the 1 is in the Units box. Why bother with a table instead of just guessing? Because with bigger numbers, or numbers with a 0 in them, it's very easy to lose track of which digit belongs where -- the table removes all doubt. Let's try a trickier one together: 3 042. Notice there's a 0 in the Hundreds place. Even though it doesn't add any value, it still holds that column open, so the 3 correctly lands in Thousands, not Hundreds. This habit -- always checking with a table when you're unsure -- will serve you well for the rest of your maths this year, especially once we start comparing and ordering bigger numbers. Let's use the table once more on a tricky case: 9 043. Draw your four boxes -- Thousands, Hundreds, Tens, Units -- and place 9, 0, 4, 3 into them from the left. The digit that trips people up here is the 0: it sits in the Hundreds box, so its place value is Hundreds, even though its actual value is zero. Many learners skip straight past a 0 and accidentally shift every other digit into the wrong column -- reading 9 043 as if it were 943. The table stops that mistake before it happens, because every digit gets its own labelled box, whether it's worth something or not. One more quick check: in 2 934, which digit sits in the Tens column? Following the same left-to-right placement, 2 is Thousands, 9 is Hundreds, 3 is Tens, and 4 is Units -- so the Tens digit is 3. Building this habit of drawing the table first, every single time, rather than trying to read a number 'in your head', will save you from careless place-value mistakes for the rest of the year.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A hand drawing four empty boxes in a row, labelling them Thousands, Hundreds, Tens, Units.
The digits of 4 371 dropping into the boxes one at a time from left to right.
Each box lighting up with its label as the answer is read aloud: 4=Thousands, 3=Hundreds, 7=Tens, 1=Units.
A second example, 3 042, showing the 0 correctly holding the Hundreds place open.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: In ons vorige les het ons ontdek dat elke syfer se posisie dit 'n ware waarde gee. Vandag verander ons daardie idee in 'n betroubare hulpmiddel wat jy enige tyd kan gebruik as jy onseker is: die plekwaardetabel self. Hier is hoe dit werk, stap vir stap. Eerste, teken vier blokke in 'n ry, en merk hulle, van links na regs, Duisende, Honderde, Tiene, Eenhede. Tweede, neem jou getal -- kom ons gebruik weer 4 371 -- en skryf elke syfer in sy eie blokkie, altyd van links af begin. Derde, lees die etiket bo elke blokkie om presies te weet wat daardie syfer beteken. Met 4 371: a) die 4 is in die Duisende-blokkie, b) die 3 is in die Honderde-blokkie, c) die 7 is in die Tiene-blokkie, en d) die 1 is in die Eenhede-blokkie. Hoekom sou jy 'n tabel gebruik in plaas daarvan om te raai? Omdat dit met groter getalle, of getalle met 'n 0 daarin, baie maklik is om spoor te verloor van watter syfer waar hoort -- die tabel verwyder alle twyfel. Kom ons probeer 'n moeiliker een saam: 3 042. Let op daar is 'n 0 in die Honderde-plek. Al voeg dit geen waarde by nie, hou dit steeds daardie kolom oop, so die 3 land korrek in Duisende, nie Honderde nie. Hierdie gewoonte -- om altyd met 'n tabel te kontroleer as jy onseker is -- sal jou goed dien vir die res van jou wiskunde vanjaar, veral sodra ons begin om groter getalle te vergelyk en te orden. Kom ons gebruik die tabel weer op 'n lastige geval: 9 043. Teken jou vier blokkies -- Duisende, Honderde, Tiene, Eenhede -- en plaas 9, 0, 4, 3 daarin van links af. Die syfer wat mense hier laat struikel is die 0: dit sit in die Honderde-blokkie, so sy plekwaarde is Honderde, al is sy werklike waarde nul. Baie leerders spring reguit verby 'n 0 en skuif per ongeluk elke ander syfer na die verkeerde kolom -- en lees 9 043 asof dit 943 was. Die tabel keer daardie fout voor dit gebeur, want elke syfer kry sy eie geëtiketteerde blokkie, of dit iets werd is of nie. Nog een vinnige kontrole: in 2 934, watter syfer sit in die Tiene-kolom? Deur dieselfde links-na-regs plasing te volg, is 2 Duisende, 9 is Honderde, 3 is Tiene, en 4 is Eenhede -- so die Tiene-syfer is 3. Om hierdie gewoonte te bou om die tabel eers te teken, elke enkele keer, eerder as om te probeer om 'n getal 'in jou kop' te lees, sal jou vir die res van die jaar van agtelose plekwaarde-foute red.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Division order matters

source_trace: 1.1. Whole numbers DIVISION Emphasize that numbers cannot be divided in any order. Example: 125 ÷ 5 ≠ 5 ÷ 125
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 24, TERM 2 Grade 4, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Understand that swapping the order of a division sum changes the answer.
Show, using an example, that 125 ÷ 5 is not the same as 5 ÷ 125.
Explain, in your own words, why order matters for division but not for addition.

english_content.narration_script: Quick question to start: does 2 plus 3 give the same answer as 3 plus 2? Of course -- both equal 5. Now here's the twist: does that same freedom apply to division? Let's find out together. Take 125 divided by 5. That means 'how many groups of 5 fit into 125?' -- and the answer is 25. Now let's flip the numbers around: 5 divided by 125 means 'how many groups of 125 fit into 5?' Since 125 is much bigger than 5, you can't even fit one whole group in -- the answer is a tiny fraction, nowhere close to 25. So 125 divided by 5 is definitely not the same as 5 divided by 125; in maths language, we write 125 ÷ 5 ≠ 5 ÷ 125. This is one of the most important rules to remember about division: unlike addition, where you can swap the numbers freely, division always depends on which number comes first. Think about it in real life: if you have 125 sweets to share among 5 friends, each friend gets 25 sweets. But if you tried to share 5 sweets among 125 friends, each person would only get a tiny sliver -- a completely different, much smaller result. That's why the order in a division sum is never something you can casually swap around, the way you might with addition or multiplication. Keep this rule in mind every time you write a division sum -- the first number is always the total amount, and the second number is always how many groups you're sharing it into. Let's test this rule on one more pair of numbers: 40 and 8. Calculate 40 divided by 8 first -- how many groups of 8 fit into 40? Exactly 5. Now flip it: 8 divided by 40 -- how many groups of 40 fit into 8? Since 40 is bigger than 8, not even one whole group fits, so the answer is a small fraction, nothing like 5. Once again, swapping the order completely changes the result. This matters because addition and multiplication can trick you into assuming every operation works the same way -- but division and subtraction don't follow that swapping rule at all. A good habit going forward: before you swap two numbers around in any calculation, ask yourself whether you're adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing, because the answer to 'does order matter here?' genuinely depends on which operation you're using. Keep this distinction in mind, and you'll avoid one of the most common mistakes learners make when they first meet division.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vinnige vraag om te begin: gee 2 plus 3 dieselfde antwoord as 3 plus 2? Natuurlik -- albei is gelyk aan 5. Hier is nou die kinkel: geld daardie vryheid ook vir deling? Kom ons vind saam uit. Neem 125 gedeel deur 5. Dit beteken 'hoeveel groepe van 5 pas in 125?' -- en die antwoord is 25. Kom ons draai nou die getalle om: 5 gedeel deur 125 beteken 'hoeveel groepe van 125 pas in 5?' Aangesien 125 baie groter as 5 is, pas jy nie eens een volle groep in nie -- die antwoord is 'n klein breukdeel, glad nie naby 25 nie. So 125 gedeel deur 5 is beslis nie dieselfde as 5 gedeel deur 125 nie; in wiskundetaal skryf ons 125 ÷ 5 ≠ 5 ÷ 125. Dit is een van die belangrikste reëls om oor deling te onthou: anders as optel, waar jy die getalle vrylik kan omruil, hang deling altyd af van watter getal eerste kom. Dink daaraan in die alledaagse lewe: as jy 125 lekkers het om onder 5 vriende te deel, kry elke vriend 25 lekkers. Maar as jy probeer om 5 lekkers onder 125 vriende te deel, sou elke persoon net 'n baie klein stukkie kry -- 'n heeltemal ander, baie kleiner uitkoms. Dit is hoekom die volgorde in 'n delingsom nooit iets is wat jy sommer kan omruil nie, soos jy dalk met optel of vermenigvuldiging sou doen. Onthou hierdie reël elke keer as jy 'n delingsom skryf -- die eerste getal is altyd die totale hoeveelheid, en die tweede getal is altyd hoeveel groepe jy dit onder verdeel. Kom ons toets hierdie reël op nog 'n paar getalle: 40 en 8. Bereken eers 40 gedeel deur 8 -- hoeveel groepe van 8 pas in 40? Presies 5. Draai dit nou om: 8 gedeel deur 40 -- hoeveel groepe van 40 pas in 8? Aangesien 40 groter as 8 is, pas nie eens een volle groep in nie, so die antwoord is 'n klein breukdeel, niks soos 5 nie. Weer eens verander die omruil van die volgorde die uitkoms heeltemal. Dit maak saak omdat optel en vermenigvuldiging jou kan mislei om aan te neem elke bewerking werk dieselfde -- maar deling en aftrekking volg glad nie daardie omruil-reël nie. 'n Goeie gewoonte om voortaan te hê: voordat jy twee getalle in enige berekening omruil, vra jouself of jy optel, aftrek, vermenigvuldig, of deel, want die antwoord op 'maak volgorde hier saak?' hang werklik af van watter bewerking jy gebruik. Hou hierdie onderskeid in gedagte, en jy sal een van die algemeenste foute vermy wat leerders maak wanneer hulle deling die eerste keer teëkom.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Dividing using a number line

source_trace: 1.1. Whole numbers Number lines Example: calculate: 192 ÷ 8, and 8 ÷ 2 = 4 shown via repeated subtraction (−2−2−2−2 = 0)
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 24, TERM 2 Grade 4, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Use repeated subtraction on a number line to work out a division fact.
Connect the number of 'jumps back' on a number line to the answer of a division.
Work backwards from the number of jumps and jump size on a number line to find the original number being divided.

english_content.narration_script: Here's a fun way to picture division: jumping backwards on a number line. Let's try it with 8 divided by 2. Start at 8 on your number line. Now, instead of counting up like usual, we're going to jump backwards in steps of 2. First jump: 8 down to 6. Second jump: 6 down to 4. Third jump: 4 down to 2. Fourth jump: 2 down to 0. We landed exactly on zero, and it took us 4 jumps to get there. That's exactly what 8 divided by 2 equals 4 means -- how many groups of 2 can you subtract from 8 before you reach zero? The answer is the number of jumps: 4. Let's try a slightly bigger challenge together: how would we picture 192 divided by 8 this way? We'd start at 192, and keep jumping back by 8, again and again, counting every jump, until we land on zero -- that would take 24 jumps in total, since 8 times 24 equals 192. That's a lot of jumps for a number line, which is exactly why, once numbers get bigger, we'll want faster methods too -- but the number-line picture is brilliant for really understanding what division actually means underneath all the shortcuts: repeatedly taking away equal groups until nothing is left. Whenever a division answer feels confusing, come back to this number-line picture, and count the jumps. Let's practise the same jumping idea with 12 divided by 3. Start at 12, and jump backwards in steps of 3: 12 to 9, 9 to 6, 6 to 3, 3 to 0. That's 4 jumps, so 12 divided by 3 equals 4. Now let's try it the other way around: if it takes exactly 6 jumps of size 4 to land on 0, what number did we start at? Working forwards, 6 jumps of 4 add up to 6 times 4, which is 24 -- so we must have started at 24. This 'jumps times jump size' idea is really just multiplication hiding inside division, and it shows you the two operations are close relatives: division asks how many jumps it takes, while multiplication tells you how far those jumps travel altogether. As numbers grow, drawing every single jump becomes impractical, but the picture in your mind -- backwards jumps, equal in size, landing exactly on zero -- stays exactly the same, and it's a picture worth holding onto whenever a division question feels confusing.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Hier is 'n prettige manier om deling voor te stel: agteruit spring op 'n getallelyn. Kom ons probeer dit met 8 gedeel deur 2. Begin by 8 op jou getallelyn. In plaas daarvan om soos gewoonlik op te tel, gaan ons nou agteruit spring in stappe van 2. Eerste sprong: 8 af na 6. Tweede sprong: 6 af na 4. Derde sprong: 4 af na 2. Vierde sprong: 2 af na 0. Ons het presies op nul geland, en dit het 4 spronge geneem om daar te kom. Dit is presies wat 8 gedeel deur 2 is gelyk aan 4 beteken -- hoeveel groepe van 2 kan jy van 8 aftrek voordat jy nul bereik? Die antwoord is die aantal spronge: 4. Kom ons probeer 'n effens groter uitdaging saam: hoe sou ons 192 gedeel deur 8 op hierdie manier voorstel? Ons sou by 192 begin, en aanhou agteruit spring met 8, weer en weer, elke sprong tel, totdat ons op nul land -- dit sou altesaam 24 spronge neem, aangesien 8 keer 24 gelyk is aan 192. Dit is baie spronge vir 'n getallelyn, en dit is presies hoekom ons, sodra getalle groter word, ook vinniger metodes wil hê -- maar die getallelyn-prentjie is uitstekend om regtig te verstaan wat deling eintlik beteken onder al die kortpaaie: herhaaldelik gelyke groepe wegneem totdat niks oorbly nie. Wanneer 'n delingsantwoord verwarrend voel, kom terug na hierdie getallelyn-prentjie, en tel die spronge. Kom ons oefen dieselfde spring-idee met 12 gedeel deur 3. Begin by 12, en spring agteruit in stappe van 3: 12 na 9, 9 na 6, 6 na 3, 3 na 0. Dit is 4 spronge, so 12 gedeel deur 3 is gelyk aan 4. Kom ons probeer dit nou andersom: as dit presies 6 spronge van grootte 4 neem om op 0 te land, watter getal het ons by begin? Deur vorentoe te werk, tel 6 spronge van 4 op tot 6 keer 4, wat 24 is -- so ons moes by 24 begin het. Hierdie 'spronge keer sprong-grootte'-idee is eintlik net vermenigvuldiging wat binne deling wegkruip, en dit wys jou die twee bewerkings is nabye verwante: deling vra hoeveel spronge dit neem, terwyl vermenigvuldiging jou vertel hoe ver daardie spronge altesaam reis. Namate getalle groei, word om elke enkele sprong te teken onprakties, maar die prentjie in jou gedagtes -- agteruit spronge, gelyk in grootte, wat presies op nul land -- bly presies dieselfde, en dit is 'n prentjie wat die moeite werd is om vas te hou wanneer 'n delingsvraag verwarrend voel.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Even and odd numbers

source_trace: 1.1. whole numbers compare even and odd numbers. examples: even and odd numbers a) 376
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 24, TERM 2 Grade 4, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Tell the difference between an even number and an odd number.
Decide whether a given whole number, like 376, is even or odd, and explain why.
Compare two numbers to say which is even and which is odd.

english_content.narration_script: Numbers come in two families: even and odd. An even number is any number you can share exactly between two people with nothing left over -- like 4, 10, or 376. An odd number always leaves one behind when you try to share it into two equal groups -- like 5, 11, or 377. Here's a secret shortcut: you don't need to share out the whole number to know which family it belongs to -- you only need to look at its very last digit. If the last digit is 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, the whole number is even. If it's 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9, the whole number is odd. Let's test this with 376. What's the last digit? It's 6. Is 6 an even digit? Yes -- so 376 is even. Let's compare two numbers together: 245 and 632. 245 ends in 5, an odd digit, so 245 is odd. 632 ends in 2, an even digit, so 632 is even. Notice we didn't need to look at the hundreds or tens digits at all -- only the very last one matters. This little trick works no matter how big the number is: even a number with ten digits can be checked for even or odd in a single glance at its last digit. Understanding even and odd numbers isn't just a fun fact either -- it's the foundation for later ideas like halving numbers evenly, sharing things fairly, and spotting number patterns. Let's use this trick on one more pair: 249 and 510. 249 ends in 9, which is odd, so 249 is odd. Notice too that 510 ends in 0, which is even, so 510 is even -- and remember, this trick doesn't care whether the number is 3 digits or 30 digits, only its last digit matters. Now here's a fun question to think about: what happens when you add two even numbers together, like 4 and 10? 4 plus 10 equals 14, which is even. Try another pair: 20 plus 6 equals 26, also even. It turns out adding two even numbers always gives an even answer -- a genuine pattern, not a coincidence. You can even see why, using our last-digit trick: an even number always ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, and adding two of those last digits together will always land back on an even digit too. This is a nice example of how a simple rule -- check the last digit -- can unlock much bigger discoveries about how numbers behave when you combine them.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Getalle kom in twee families: ewe en onewe. 'n Ewe getal is enige getal wat jy presies tussen twee mense kan deel sonder iets oor -- soos 4, 10, of 376. 'n Onewe getal laat altyd een oor wanneer jy dit probeer deel in twee gelyke groepe -- soos 5, 11, of 377. Hier is 'n geheime kortpad: jy hoef nie die hele getal uit te deel om te weet aan watter familie dit behoort nie -- jy hoef net na sy heel laaste syfer te kyk. As die laaste syfer 0, 2, 4, 6, of 8 is, is die hele getal ewe. As dit 1, 3, 5, 7, of 9 is, is die hele getal onewe. Kom ons toets dit met 376. Wat is die laaste syfer? Dit is 6. Is 6 'n ewe syfer? Ja -- so 376 is ewe. Kom ons vergelyk twee getalle saam: 245 en 632. 245 eindig op 5, 'n onewe syfer, so 245 is onewe. 632 eindig op 2, 'n ewe syfer, so 632 is ewe. Let op ons hoef glad nie na die honderde- of tiene-syfer te kyk nie -- net die heel laaste een tel. Hierdie klein truuk werk maak nie saak hoe groot die getal is nie: selfs 'n getal met tien syfers kan met net een oogopslag op sy laaste syfer as ewe of onewe nagegaan word. Om ewe en onewe getalle te verstaan is ook nie net 'n prettige feit nie -- dit is die grondslag vir later idees soos om getalle ewe te halveer, dinge regverdig te deel, en getalpatrone raak te sien. Kom ons gebruik hierdie truuk op nog 'n paar: 249 en 510. 249 eindig op 9, wat onewe is, so 249 is onewe. Let ook op 510 eindig op 0, wat ewe is, so 510 is ewe -- en onthou, hierdie truuk gee nie om of die getal 3 syfers of 30 syfers het nie, net sy laaste syfer tel. Hier is nou 'n interessante vraag om oor na te dink: wat gebeur wanneer jy twee ewe getalle bymekaar tel, soos 4 en 10? 4 plus 10 is gelyk aan 14, wat ewe is. Probeer nog 'n paar: 20 plus 6 is gelyk aan 26, ook ewe. Dit blyk dat om twee ewe getalle bymekaar te tel altyd 'n ewe antwoord gee -- 'n ware patroon, nie 'n toeval nie. Jy kan selfs sien hoekom, deur ons laaste-syfer-truuk te gebruik: 'n ewe getal eindig altyd op 0, 2, 4, 6, of 8, en om twee van daardie laaste syfers bymekaar te tel sal altyd weer op 'n ewe syfer land. Dit is 'n mooi voorbeeld van hoe 'n eenvoudige reël -- kontroleer die laaste syfer -- baie groter ontdekkings kan ontsluit oor hoe getalle hulle gedra wanneer jy hulle kombineer.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Halving 1-, 2- and 3-digit numbers

source_trace: 1.1. Whole numbers Halving 1, 2 and 3 digit numbers. Halve 1, 2 and 3-digit numbers. Example: Half of 54 = 27, half of 168 = 84 and half of 500 = 250
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 24, TERM 2 Grade 4, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Find half of a 1-, 2- or 3-digit whole number using mental maths.
Explain that 'half of' a number is the same as dividing that number by 2.
Use a splitting strategy to halve bigger numbers more easily.

english_content.narration_script: Halving is one of the most useful everyday maths skills -- it's exactly what happens when you split something fairly between two people. 'Half of a number' simply means dividing that number by 2. Let's start small: half of 8 means 8 divided by 2, which is 4 -- if you split 8 sweets fairly between two friends, each friend gets 4. Now let's try a bigger number: half of 54. A clever trick is to split the number into friendlier pieces first. 54 splits nicely into 50 and 4. Half of 50 is 25, and half of 4 is 2. Add those together: 25 plus 2 equals 27. So half of 54 is 27. Let's try an even bigger one: half of 168. Split it into 160 and 8. Half of 160 is 80, and half of 8 is 4. Add them: 80 plus 4 equals 84. So half of 168 is 84. And one more, an easy one: half of 500. Since 250 plus 250 equals 500, half of 500 is simply 250. Notice the pattern in our strategy: whenever a number feels too big to halve all at once, split it into two friendlier chunks, halve each chunk separately, then add the results back together. This same splitting idea will come back again and again in maths, so it's well worth practising now with numbers you can check easily. Let's try one more together using this splitting trick: half of 250. Split 250 into 200 and 50. Half of 200 is 100, and half of 50 is 25. Add them: 100 plus 25 equals 125. So half of 250 is 125. Now let's work backwards for a change: if half of a number is 36, what was the original number? Since halving means dividing by 2, the reverse operation is doubling -- multiplying by 2. So double 36: 36 plus 36 equals 72. The original number was 72, and you can check it: half of 72 is indeed 36. This 'doubling to undo halving' idea is a genuinely useful checking strategy -- whenever you halve a number, you can always confirm your answer is correct by doubling it back and seeing if you land on the number you started with. Try building this checking habit now, because it will save you from careless mistakes on every halving question you meet from here on.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Halvering is een van die nuttigste alledaagse wiskundevaardighede -- dit is presies wat gebeur wanneer jy iets regverdig tussen twee mense verdeel. 'Helfte van 'n getal' beteken eenvoudig om daardie getal deur 2 te deel. Kom ons begin klein: helfte van 8 beteken 8 gedeel deur 2, wat 4 is -- as jy 8 lekkers regverdig tussen twee vriende verdeel, kry elke vriend 4. Kom ons probeer nou 'n groter getal: helfte van 54. 'n Slim truuk is om die getal eers in vriendeliker stukke te verdeel. 54 verdeel netjies in 50 en 4. Helfte van 50 is 25, en helfte van 4 is 2. Tel dit bymekaar: 25 plus 2 is gelyk aan 27. So helfte van 54 is 27. Kom ons probeer 'n nog groter een: helfte van 168. Verdeel dit in 160 en 8. Helfte van 160 is 80, en helfte van 8 is 4. Tel hulle bymekaar: 80 plus 4 is gelyk aan 84. So helfte van 168 is 84. En nog een, 'n maklike een: helfte van 500. Aangesien 250 plus 250 gelyk is aan 500, is helfte van 500 eenvoudig 250. Let op die patroon in ons strategie: wanneer 'n getal te groot voel om op een slag te halveer, verdeel dit in twee vriendeliker stukke, halveer elke stuk apart, en tel dan die resultate weer bymekaar. Hierdie selfde verdelingsidee sal weer en weer in wiskunde terugkom, so dit is die moeite werd om dit nou te oefen met getalle wat jy maklik kan nagaan. Kom ons probeer nog een saam met hierdie verdelingstruuk: helfte van 250. Verdeel 250 in 200 en 50. Helfte van 200 is 100, en helfte van 50 is 25. Tel dit bymekaar: 100 plus 25 is gelyk aan 125. So helfte van 250 is 125. Kom ons werk nou vir 'n verandering agteruit: as helfte van 'n getal 36 is, wat was die oorspronklike getal? Aangesien halvering beteken om deur 2 te deel, is die omgekeerde bewerking verdubbeling -- vermenigvuldig met 2. So verdubbel 36: 36 plus 36 is gelyk aan 72. Die oorspronklike getal was 72, en jy kan dit nagaan: helfte van 72 is inderdaad 36. Hierdie 'verdubbel om halvering ongedaan te maak'-idee is 'n werklik nuttige kontrolestrategie -- wanneer jy ook al 'n getal halveer, kan jy altyd bevestig jou antwoord is korrek deur dit terug te verdubbel en te sien of jy op die getal land waarmee jy begin het. Probeer hierdie kontrolegewoonte nou bou, want dit sal jou van agtelose foute red op elke halveringsvraag wat jy van hier af teëkom.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Mental division using multiplication tables

source_trace: 1.1. Whole numbers Mental mathematics: Calculate quotients using knowledge of multiplication tables. Example: a) 72 ÷ 9 = 8 b) 74 ÷ 9 = 8 remainder 2 c) 132 ÷ 12 = 11
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 24, TERM 2 Grade 4, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Use known multiplication facts to work out a division answer quickly, in your head.
Solve division problems that come out exactly, and ones that leave a remainder.
Turn a division question into a multiplication question to solve it faster.

english_content.narration_script: Here's a secret that will make division much faster: you don't need brand new facts for division if you already know your multiplication tables. Division and multiplication are two sides of the same coin. Let's try 72 divided by 9. Instead of working it out from scratch, ask yourself: '9 times what number gives 72?' If you know your 9 times table, you'll remember that 9 times 8 equals 72 -- so 72 divided by 9 equals 8. Now let's try one that doesn't come out perfectly evenly: 74 divided by 9. Using the same trick, the closest fact you know is 9 times 8 equals 72. But we need 74, and 72 is 2 short of that. So 74 divided by 9 equals 8, with 2 left over -- we write that as '8 remainder 2'. One more example: 132 divided by 12. Think: '12 times what gives 132?' If you know that 12 times 11 equals 132, then you instantly know 132 divided by 12 equals 11. Notice the pattern in all three examples: we never actually 'did' the division the hard way -- we simply asked a multiplication question we already knew the answer to, or nearly knew, and worked backwards. Whenever you're stuck on a division question, try flipping it into a multiplication question using the tables you've already memorised -- it's often much faster than any other method. Let's flip a known multiplication fact into a division answer one more time. If you already know that 8 times 9 equals 72, that single fact actually hands you two division facts for free: 72 divided by 8 equals 9, and 72 divided by 9 equals 8. This is one of the most powerful shortcuts in mental maths -- every multiplication fact you've memorised is secretly two division facts in disguise, just waiting to be read the other way around. Let's try one more with a remainder: 50 divided by 6. The closest fact you know is 6 times 8 equals 48. Since 50 is 2 more than 48, the answer is 8 remainder 2. Notice the process never changes: find the closest multiplication fact below your number, subtract to find the gap, and that gap becomes your remainder. The better you know your times tables, the faster this whole process becomes, which is exactly why mental division rewards the time you've already spent memorising multiplication facts in earlier grades.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A 9-times table chart with '9 x 8 = 72' highlighted, then an arrow looping to show '72 ÷ 9 = 8' as the same fact backwards.
74 objects being grouped into 8 full groups of 9 with 2 objects left over outside the groups.
A 12-times table chart highlighting '12 x 11 = 132', with an arrow showing '132 ÷ 12 = 11'.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Hier is 'n geheim wat deling baie vinniger sal maak: jy het nie splinternuwe feite vir deling nodig as jy reeds jou vermenigvuldigingstafels ken nie. Deling en vermenigvuldiging is twee kante van dieselfde munt. Kom ons probeer 72 gedeel deur 9. In plaas daarvan om dit van voor af uit te werk, vra jouself: '9 keer watter getal gee 72?' As jy jou 9-tafel ken, sal jy onthou dat 9 keer 8 gelyk is aan 72 -- so 72 gedeel deur 9 is gelyk aan 8. Kom ons probeer nou een wat nie perfek eweredig uitkom nie: 74 gedeel deur 9. Met dieselfde truuk is die naaste feit wat jy ken 9 keer 8 gelyk aan 72. Maar ons het 74 nodig, en 72 is 2 kort daarvan. So 74 gedeel deur 9 is gelyk aan 8, met 2 oor -- ons skryf dit as '8 oor 2'. Nog 'n voorbeeld: 132 gedeel deur 12. Dink: '12 keer wat gee 132?' As jy weet dat 12 keer 11 gelyk is aan 132, weet jy dadelik dat 132 gedeel deur 12 gelyk is aan 11. Let op die patroon in al drie voorbeelde: ons het nooit werklik die deling op die moeilike manier 'gedoen' nie -- ons het bloot 'n vermenigvuldigingsvraag gevra waarvan ons reeds die antwoord geken het, of amper geken het, en agteruit gewerk. Wanneer jy vasval op 'n delingsvraag, probeer dit omdraai in 'n vermenigvuldigingsvraag deur die tafels wat jy reeds uit jou kop ken -- dit is dikwels baie vinniger as enige ander metode. Kom ons draai 'n bekende vermenigvuldigingsfeit nog een keer om na 'n delingsantwoord. As jy reeds weet dat 8 keer 9 gelyk is aan 72, gee daardie enkele feit jou eintlik gratis twee delingsfeite: 72 gedeel deur 8 is gelyk aan 9, en 72 gedeel deur 9 is gelyk aan 8. Dit is een van die kragtigste kortpaaie in verstandelike wiskunde -- elke vermenigvuldigingsfeit wat jy gememoriseer het, is stilweg twee delingsfeite vermom, wat net wag om andersom gelees te word. Kom ons probeer nog een met 'n oorskot: 50 gedeel deur 6. Die naaste feit wat jy ken is 6 keer 8 is gelyk aan 48. Aangesien 50 2 meer as 48 is, is die antwoord 8 oor 2. Let op die proses verander nooit: vind die naaste vermenigvuldigingsfeit onder jou getal, trek af om die gaping te vind, en daardie gaping word jou oorskot. Hoe beter jy jou tafels ken, hoe vinniger word hierdie hele proses, wat presies hoekom verstandelike deling die tyd beloon wat jy reeds in vorige grade spandeer het om vermenigvuldigingsfeite te memoriseer.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Dividing a 3-digit number by a 1-digit number (breaking-down technique)

source_trace: Divide whole numbers with at least 3 digits by 1-digit whole numbers. Example: Calculate: 192 ÷ 8 By breaking down technique. Write 192 as the sum of multiples of 8 (192 = 160 + 32); 32 ÷ 8 = 4 and 16
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 24, TERM 2 Grade 4, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Divide a 3-digit whole number by a 1-digit whole number using the breaking-down technique.
Break a number into two friendly multiples of the divisor, then combine the results.
Explain why breaking a number into two friendly parts before dividing still gives the correct final answer.

english_content.narration_script: Big division problems feel much easier once you break the big number into smaller, friendlier pieces, then add the answers back together. Let's work through 192 divided by 8 together, using exactly this idea. First, we need to split 192 into two numbers that are both easy multiples of 8. Let's try 160 and 32, since 160 plus 32 equals 192. Why those two? Because 160 divided by 8 is a friendly 20, and 32 divided by 8 is a friendly 4 -- both easy facts. Now divide each piece separately: 160 divided by 8 equals 20, and 32 divided by 8 equals 4. Finally, add those two answers together: 20 plus 4 equals 24. So 192 divided by 8 equals 24. Here's why this trick actually works: division shares out evenly across addition, which means as long as your two pieces genuinely add up to the original number, dividing each piece separately and adding the results gives you exactly the same answer as dividing the whole number at once. The real skill here isn't the adding at the end -- it's choosing good pieces to split into, ones that are both easy multiples of your divisor. With practice, you'll start spotting friendly splits almost instantly. Let's try one more together: 156 divided by 4. We need two friendly multiples of 4 that add up to 156. Let's use 120 and 36, since 120 plus 36 equals 156. Divide each piece: 120 divided by 4 equals 30, and 36 divided by 4 equals 9. Add the results: 30 plus 9 equals 39. So 156 divided by 4 equals 39. Notice there's often more than one valid way to split a number -- we could just as easily have used 100 and 56 instead of 120 and 36, and still arrived at the same final answer, as long as both pieces divide evenly by 4. This flexibility is actually a strength of the breaking-down technique: there's no single 'correct' way to split a number, only splits that make the arithmetic easier for you personally. As you practise more examples, you'll develop an instinct for which splits feel quickest, usually ones involving round numbers like 100, 120, or 200 that you can divide in your head almost instantly.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: The number 192 splitting apart into two labelled chunks, '160' and '32'.
Each chunk with a division arrow pointing to 8, showing '160 ÷ 8 = 20' and '32 ÷ 8 = 4'.
The two results, 20 and 4, joining together into the final answer 24.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Groot delingsprobleme voel baie makliker sodra jy die groot getal in kleiner, vriendeliker stukke verdeel, en dan die antwoorde weer bymekaar tel. Kom ons werk saam deur 192 gedeel deur 8, met presies hierdie idee. Eerste moet ons 192 in twee getalle verdeel wat albei maklike veelvoude van 8 is. Kom ons probeer 160 en 32, aangesien 160 plus 32 gelyk is aan 192. Hoekom daardie twee? Omdat 160 gedeel deur 8 'n vriendelike 20 is, en 32 gedeel deur 8 'n vriendelike 4 is -- albei maklike feite. Deel nou elke stuk apart: 160 gedeel deur 8 is gelyk aan 20, en 32 gedeel deur 8 is gelyk aan 4. Laastens, tel daardie twee antwoorde bymekaar: 20 plus 4 is gelyk aan 24. So 192 gedeel deur 8 is gelyk aan 24. Hier is hoekom hierdie truuk eintlik werk: deling deel eweredig oor optel, wat beteken solank jou twee stukke werklik optel tot die oorspronklike getal, gee die aparte deling van elke stuk en die optel van die resultate presies dieselfde antwoord as om die hele getal op een slag te deel. Die ware vaardigheid hier is nie die optel aan die einde nie -- dit is om goeie stukke te kies om in te verdeel, stukke wat albei maklike veelvoude van jou deler is. Met oefening sal jy amper onmiddellik vriendelike verdelings begin raaksien. Kom ons probeer nog een saam: 156 gedeel deur 4. Ons het twee vriendelike veelvoude van 4 nodig wat optel tot 156. Kom ons gebruik 120 en 36, aangesien 120 plus 36 gelyk is aan 156. Deel elke stuk: 120 gedeel deur 4 is gelyk aan 30, en 36 gedeel deur 4 is gelyk aan 9. Tel die resultate: 30 plus 9 is gelyk aan 39. So 156 gedeel deur 4 is gelyk aan 39. Let op daar is dikwels meer as een geldige manier om 'n getal te verdeel -- ons kon net so maklik 100 en 56 in plaas van 120 en 36 gebruik het, en steeds by dieselfde finale antwoord uitgekom het, solank albei stukke eweredig deur 4 deel. Hierdie buigsaamheid is eintlik 'n sterkpunt van die afbreek-tegniek: daar is geen enkele 'korrekte' manier om 'n getal te verdeel nie, net verdelings wat die rekenkunde vir jou persoonlik makliker maak. Namate jy meer voorbeelde oefen, sal jy 'n instink ontwikkel vir watter verdelings die vinnigste voel, gewoonlik dié met ronde getalle soos 100, 120, of 200 wat jy amper onmiddellik in jou kop kan deel.

learning_objectives: Name the main skills covered in this Whole Numbers unit.
See how the smaller skills (division order, halving, mental maths) fit together under one unit.
Distinguish between the unit's overall heading and the individual skills grouped beneath it.

english_content.narration_script: This lesson is a little different from the others -- it's the title page for everything we've learned in this Whole Numbers section, rather than a brand new skill on its own. Let's recap the full journey together. We started by learning that division order matters -- 125 divided by 5 is not the same as 5 divided by 125. Then we pictured division on a number line, jumping backwards in equal steps. We compared even and odd numbers, discovering the last-digit trick. We practised halving 1-, 2- and 3-digit numbers by splitting them into friendly pieces. We used our multiplication tables to divide mentally, even when there's a remainder. And finally, we tackled dividing a 3-digit number by a single digit using the breaking-down technique. Notice how all six of these skills share one big theme: understanding whole numbers deeply enough to work with them flexibly, not just by following one fixed method. Think of '1.1 Whole Numbers' as the name of the whole folder, and each of those six skills as a document inside it. As you move into the next unit, try to notice how these Whole Numbers skills -- especially breaking numbers into friendly pieces -- keep showing up again in new situations throughout the year. Let's walk through why grouping these six skills together actually makes sense. Division order, number-line division, and mental division with the times tables are all different ways of asking the same underlying question: 'how many equal groups fit into this number?' Even and odd numbers, meanwhile, connect closely to halving, since an even number is exactly one that halves perfectly, with nothing left over. And the breaking-down technique for 3-digit division pulls together everything else -- it uses your knowledge of friendly multiples, which relies on knowing your times tables well, which in turn depends on being comfortable with even and odd numbers and place value from earlier lessons. So while '1.1 Whole Numbers' might look like just a heading on a page, it actually represents one connected web of number sense, where each smaller skill supports and strengthens the others. When you revise for a test, it often helps to revise this way -- not skill by skill in isolation, but by tracing how each one connects to and depends on the others around it.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Hierdie les is 'n bietjie anders as die ander -- dit is die titelblad vir alles wat ons in hierdie Heelgetalle-afdeling geleer het, eerder as 'n splinternuwe vaardigheid op sy eie. Kom ons gaan saam deur die volle reis. Ons het begin deur te leer dat delingsvolgorde saak maak -- 125 gedeel deur 5 is nie dieselfde as 5 gedeel deur 125 nie. Toe het ons deling op 'n getallelyn voorgestel, deur agteruit te spring in gelyke stappe. Ons het ewe en onewe getalle vergelyk, en die laaste-syfer-truuk ontdek. Ons het geoefen om 1-, 2- en 3-syfergetalle te halveer deur hulle in vriendelike stukke te verdeel. Ons het ons vermenigvuldigingstafels gebruik om verstandelik te deel, selfs wanneer daar 'n oorskot is. En laastens het ons aangepak om 'n 3-syfergetal deur 'n enkele syfer te deel met die afbreek-tegniek. Let op hoe al ses hierdie vaardighede een groot tema deel: om heelgetalle diep genoeg te verstaan om buigsaam daarmee te werk, nie net deur een vaste metode te volg nie. Dink aan '1.1 Heelgetalle' as die naam van die hele lêer, en elk van daardie ses vaardighede as 'n dokument daarbinne. Terwyl jy na die volgende eenheid beweeg, probeer opmerk hoe hierdie Heelgetalle-vaardighede -- veral om getalle in vriendelike stukke te verdeel -- weer en weer in nuwe situasies regdeur die jaar sal opduik. Kom ons gaan deur hoekom om hierdie ses vaardighede saam te groepeer eintlik sin maak. Delingsvolgorde, getallelyn-deling, en verstandelike deling met die tafels is almal verskillende maniere om dieselfde onderliggende vraag te vra: 'hoeveel gelyke groepe pas in hierdie getal?' Ewe en onewe getalle, intussen, hou nou verband met halvering, aangesien 'n ewe getal presies een is wat perfek halveer, met niks oor nie. En die afbreek-tegniek vir 3-syferdeling trek alles anders saam -- dit gebruik jou kennis van vriendelike veelvoude, wat afhang van om jou tafels goed te ken, wat op sy beurt afhang van om gemaklik te wees met ewe en onewe getalle en plekwaarde van vroeëre lesse. So terwyl '1.1 Heelgetalle' dalk soos net 'n opskrif op 'n bladsy lyk, verteenwoordig dit eintlik een verbonde web van getalsin, waar elke kleiner vaardigheid die ander ondersteun en versterk. Wanneer jy vir 'n toets hersien, help dit dikwels om so te hersien -- nie vaardigheid vir vaardigheid in isolasie nie, maar deur na te spoor hoe elkeen met die ander daarom verband hou en daarvan afhang.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Place value in bigger whole numbers (up to 6 digits)

source_trace: Recognise the place values of digits in whole numbers to at least 6 digits. Example: the value of digit 7 in the number 871 253 is 7 ten thousands or 70 000
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 30, TERM 1 Grade 5, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Recognise the place value of a digit in a whole number with up to 6 digits.
Extend the Thousands-Hundreds-Tens-Units table to include Ten Thousands and Hundred Thousands.
Compare the value of a specific digit across two different numbers to determine which is larger.

english_content.narration_script: Remember our place value table from Grade 4 -- Thousands, Hundreds, Tens, Units? In Grade 5, numbers get bigger, so our table needs two more columns: Ten Thousands and Hundred Thousands. Let's use 871 253 as our example. Reading from the left: 8 sits in the Hundred Thousands column, worth 800 000. 7 sits in Ten Thousands, worth 70 000. 1 sits in Thousands, worth 1 000. 2 sits in Hundreds, worth 200. 5 sits in Tens, worth 50. And 3 sits in Units, worth 3. Add all six values together -- 800 000 plus 70 000 plus 1 000 plus 200 plus 50 plus 3 -- and you get 871 253 right back again. Let's focus on one digit specifically, since it often causes confusion: the 7 in 871 253. It sits in the Ten Thousands column, so its value is 7 ten thousands, which we can also write as 70 000. Notice the value is much bigger than the digit itself suggests -- that's the whole point of place value. As numbers grow bigger this year, this same table just keeps growing new columns on the left, but the idea never changes: find the column, read its name, and you know the digit's true worth. Let's try comparing two bigger numbers using place value: which is bigger, the value of the 4 in 41 000, or the value of the 9 in 9 800? First, find where the 4 sits in 41 000: it's in the Ten Thousands column, so it's worth 40 000. Next, find where the 9 sits in 9 800: it's in the Thousands column, so it's worth 9 000. Comparing 40 000 to 9 000, the 4 in 41 000 is worth far more, even though 9 looks like the bigger single digit. This is exactly why place value matters so much: a digit's column can completely overpower how big or small the digit itself looks. Let's also practise writing a number from its place values: if a number has 5 in the Hundred Thousands column, 2 in Tens, 1 in Units, and 0 everywhere else, we build it column by column: 500 000 plus 20 plus 1 equals 502 021. Keep practising both directions -- reading a big number into its place values, and building a big number back up from them -- since you'll need both skills constantly as numbers keep growing throughout this year.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Onthou ons plekwaardetabel van Graad 4 -- Duisende, Honderde, Tiene, Eenhede? In Graad 5 word getalle groter, so ons tabel het nog twee kolomme nodig: Tien Duisende en Honderd Duisende. Kom ons gebruik 871 253 as ons voorbeeld. Van links af gelees: 8 sit in die Honderd Duisende-kolom, 800 000 werd. 7 sit in Tien Duisende, 70 000 werd. 1 sit in Duisende, 1 000 werd. 2 sit in Honderde, 200 werd. 5 sit in Tiene, 50 werd. En 3 sit in Eenhede, 3 werd. Tel al ses waardes bymekaar -- 800 000 plus 70 000 plus 1 000 plus 200 plus 50 plus 3 -- en jy kry weer 871 253. Kom ons fokus op een syfer spesifiek, aangesien dit dikwels verwarring veroorsaak: die 7 in 871 253. Dit sit in die Tien Duisende-kolom, so sy waarde is 7 tien duisende, wat ons ook kan skryf as 70 000. Let op die waarde is baie groter as wat die syfer self voorstel -- dit is die hele punt van plekwaarde. Namate getalle vanjaar groter word, groei hierdie selfde tabel net nuwe kolomme aan die linkerkant, maar die idee verander nooit: vind die kolom, lees sy naam, en jy ken die syfer se ware waarde. Kom ons probeer twee groter getalle vergelyk met plekwaarde: watter is groter, die waarde van die 4 in 41 000, of die waarde van die 9 in 9 800? Vind eers waar die 4 in 41 000 sit: dit is in die Tien Duisende-kolom, so dit is 40 000 werd. Vind volgende waar die 9 in 9 800 sit: dit is in die Duisende-kolom, so dit is 9 000 werd. As ons 40 000 met 9 000 vergelyk, is die 4 in 41 000 baie meer werd, al lyk 9 soos die groter enkele syfer. Dit is presies hoekom plekwaarde so baie saak maak: 'n syfer se kolom kan heeltemal oorheers hoe groot of klein die syfer self lyk. Kom ons oefen ook om 'n getal van sy plekwaardes te skryf: as 'n getal 5 in die Honderd Duisende-kolom het, 2 in Tiene, 1 in Eenhede, en 0 orals anders, bou ons dit kolom vir kolom: 500 000 plus 20 plus 1 is gelyk aan 502 021. Bly albei rigtings oefen -- om 'n groot getal in sy plekwaardes te lees, en om 'n groot getal daarvandaan weer op te bou -- aangesien jy albei vaardighede voortdurend nodig sal hê namate getalle regdeur vanjaar aanhou groei.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Mental addition and subtraction strategies

source_trace: Do mental addition involving whole numbers. Examples: a) 187 + 7 = 194 b) 9 + 392 = 401. Do mental subtraction: a) 211 - 12 = 199 b) 375 - 25 = 350
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 30, TERM 1 Grade 5, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Add and subtract numbers mentally using a 'round then adjust' strategy.
Apply the same strategy to both addition and subtraction problems.
Explain why rounding to a nearby multiple of ten makes mental addition and subtraction easier.

english_content.narration_script: Let's solve 187 plus 7 in our heads, no paper needed. Instead of adding 7 straight onto 187, round 187 up to the nearest friendly number first: 190 is only 3 away. Use 3 of our 7 to get there, leaving 4 remaining. Add that leftover 4 onto 190: 190 plus 4 equals 194. So 187 plus 7 equals 194. This same 'round then adjust' trick works for subtraction too. Try 211 minus 12: round 211 down to 200 -- but wait, we're subtracting FROM 211, so instead let's break 12 into 11 plus 1, and subtract in two easy steps: 211 minus 11 equals 200, then 200 minus 1 equals 199. Either way, we land on 199. One more: 375 minus 25. Since 25 is a friendly quarter of 100, this one's fast: 375 minus 25 equals 350. Notice the common thread through all these examples: we're never doing the 'hard' calculation directly -- we're finding a nearby friendly number, and adjusting from there. The more you practise spotting friendly numbers -- multiples of 10, 100, or numbers like 25 and 50 -- the faster and more confident your mental maths becomes. Let's try one more pair together, starting with addition: 9 plus 392. Round 392 up to 400 -- that used 8 of our 9. We have 1 left over. Add that 1 onto 400: 400 plus 1 equals 401. So 9 plus 392 equals 401. Now for subtraction: 402 minus 15. Split 15 into 2 plus 13. Subtract in two friendly steps: 402 minus 2 equals 400, then 400 minus 13 equals 387. So 402 minus 15 equals 387. Notice something important in both examples: we always aim for a round number -- like 400 -- somewhere in the middle of our steps, because round numbers are the easiest to work with mentally. This is really the heart of good mental maths: instead of tackling a calculation exactly as it's written, look for a nearby round number, travel there first in an easy step, and then finish the journey with whatever small amount is left over. The more often you practise spotting these round 'stepping stones', the more naturally this strategy will come to you.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: 187 on a number line hopping +3 to reach 190, then +4 more to land on 194.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Kom ons los 187 plus 7 in ons koppe op, sonder papier. In plaas daarvan om 7 reguit op 187 by te tel, rond 187 eers op tot 'n vriendelike getal: 190 is net 3 weg. Gebruik 3 van ons 7 om daar te kom, wat 4 oorlaat. Tel daardie oorblywende 4 op 190: 190 plus 4 is gelyk aan 194. So 187 plus 7 is gelyk aan 194. Hierdie selfde 'rond dan pas aan'-truuk werk ook vir aftrekking. Probeer 211 minus 12: verdeel 12 in 11 plus 1, en trek af in twee maklike stappe: 211 minus 11 is gelyk aan 200, dan 200 minus 1 is gelyk aan 199. Op enige manier land ons op 199. Nog een: 375 minus 25. Aangesien 25 'n vriendelike kwart van 100 is, is hierdie een vinnig: 375 minus 25 is gelyk aan 350. Let op die gemeenskaplike draad deur al hierdie voorbeelde: ons doen nooit die 'moeilike' berekening direk nie -- ons vind 'n nabygeleë vriendelike getal, en pas daarvandaan aan. Hoe meer jy oefen om vriendelike getalle raak te sien -- veelvoude van 10, 100, of getalle soos 25 en 50 -- hoe vinniger en selfversekerder jou verstandelike wiskunde word. Kom ons probeer nog 'n paar saam, begin met optel: 9 plus 392. Rond 392 op tot 400 -- dit het 8 van ons 9 gebruik. Ons het 1 oor. Tel daardie 1 op 400: 400 plus 1 is gelyk aan 401. So 9 plus 392 is gelyk aan 401. Nou vir aftrekking: 402 minus 15. Verdeel 15 in 2 plus 13. Trek af in twee vriendelike stappe: 402 minus 2 is gelyk aan 400, dan 400 minus 13 is gelyk aan 387. So 402 minus 15 is gelyk aan 387. Let op iets belangriks in albei voorbeelde: ons mik altyd na 'n ronde getal -- soos 400 -- iewers in die middel van ons stappe, aangesien ronde getalle die maklikste is om verstandelik mee te werk. Dit is regtig die hart van goeie verstandelike wiskunde: eerder as om 'n berekening presies aan te pak soos dit geskryf is, soek 'n nabygeleë ronde getal, reis daarheen eers in 'n maklike stap, en voltooi dan die reis met watter klein bedrag ook al oorbly. Hoe meer gereeld jy oefen om hierdie ronde 'trapklippe' raak te sien, hoe natuurliker sal hierdie strategie na jou toe kom.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Dividing a 3-digit number by a 2-digit number

source_trace: Divide whole numbers with at least 3 digits by 2-digit whole numbers. Examples: a) Calculate 266 ÷ 7... c) factor method: 680 ÷ 20 = 680÷10÷2 = 34, 736÷16 = 736÷8÷2 = 46
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 36, TERM 2 Grade 5, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Divide a 3-digit whole number by a 2-digit whole number.
Use the factor method: split the divisor into two smaller factors and divide by each in turn.
Explain why splitting a divisor into two factors and dividing by each in turn gives the correct answer.

english_content.narration_script: You already know how to break a number into friendly pieces to divide by a single digit -- now let's divide by a 2-digit number instead, using a clever trick called the factor method. Let's try 680 divided by 20. Instead of dividing by 20 directly, notice that 20 equals 10 times 2. So we can divide by 10 first, then by 2. 680 divided by 10 equals 68. Then 68 divided by 2 equals 34. So 680 divided by 20 equals 34 -- and we never had to divide by 20 directly at all! Let's try a trickier one: 736 divided by 16. Notice 16 equals 8 times 2. Divide by 8 first: 736 divided by 8 equals 92. Then divide by 2: 92 divided by 2 equals 46. So 736 divided by 16 equals 46. The factor method works because dividing by a number is the same as dividing by its factors one after another -- splitting one hard division into two easier ones. The trick is spotting useful factor pairs: 20 as 10 times 2, or 16 as 8 times 2, or even 4 times 4. With practice, you'll start seeing these useful splits automatically whenever you face a 2-digit divisor. Let's practise once more with 900 divided by 18. Notice 18 equals 9 times 2. Divide by 9 first: 900 divided by 9 equals 100. Then divide by 2: 100 divided by 2 equals 50. So 900 divided by 18 equals 50. It's worth noticing that 18 could also be split as 6 times 3, or even 18 as 3 times 3 times 2 -- there's often more than one valid factor pair to choose from, and any correct split will lead you to the same final answer. So why does splitting a divisor into factors and dividing by each one actually work? Think of it this way: dividing by 18 all at once is the same as first sharing something into 2 equal groups, and then sharing each of those groups again into 9 equal groups -- you end up with exactly the same total number of small groups either way, which is 18 groups altogether. Choosing the friendliest factor pair -- usually one involving 2, 5, or 10 -- is what makes this method genuinely faster than dividing by the full 2-digit number directly.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: 680 dividing by 10 first (landing on 68), then that result dividing by 2 (landing on 34).
736 dividing by 8 first (landing on 92), then that result dividing by 2 (landing on 46).
A simple diagram showing 20 splitting into 10 x 2, and 16 splitting into 8 x 2.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Jy weet reeds hoe om 'n getal in vriendelike stukke te verdeel om deur 'n enkele syfer te deel -- kom ons deel nou deur 'n 2-syfergetal, deur 'n slim truuk genoem die faktormetode te gebruik. Kom ons probeer 680 gedeel deur 20. In plaas daarvan om direk deur 20 te deel, let op dat 20 gelyk is aan 10 keer 2. So ons kan eers deur 10 deel, dan deur 2. 680 gedeel deur 10 is gelyk aan 68. Dan 68 gedeel deur 2 is gelyk aan 34. So 680 gedeel deur 20 is gelyk aan 34 -- en ons hoef nooit direk deur 20 te deel nie! Kom ons probeer 'n moeiliker een: 736 gedeel deur 16. Let op 16 is gelyk aan 8 keer 2. Deel eers deur 8: 736 gedeel deur 8 is gelyk aan 92. Deel dan deur 2: 92 gedeel deur 2 is gelyk aan 46. So 736 gedeel deur 16 is gelyk aan 46. Die faktormetode werk omdat om deur 'n getal te deel dieselfde is as om agtereenvolgens deur sy faktore te deel -- een moeilike deling in twee makliker delings verdeel. Die truuk is om nuttige faktorpare raak te sien: 20 as 10 keer 2, of 16 as 8 keer 2, of selfs 4 keer 4. Met oefening sal jy hierdie nuttige verdelings outomaties begin raaksien wanneer jy 'n 2-syferdeler teëkom. Kom ons oefen nog een keer met 900 gedeel deur 18. Let op 18 is gelyk aan 9 keer 2. Deel eers deur 9: 900 gedeel deur 9 is gelyk aan 100. Deel dan deur 2: 100 gedeel deur 2 is gelyk aan 50. So 900 gedeel deur 18 is gelyk aan 50. Dit is die moeite werd om op te let dat 18 ook as 6 keer 3 verdeel kon word, of selfs 18 as 3 keer 3 keer 2 -- daar is dikwels meer as een geldige faktorpaar om uit te kies, en enige korrekte verdeling sal jou na dieselfde finale antwoord lei. So hoekom werk om 'n deler in faktore te verdeel en deur elkeen te deel eintlik? Dink daaraan so: om deur 18 op een slag te deel is dieselfde as om eers iets in 2 gelyke groepe te deel, en dan elkeen van daardie groepe weer in 9 gelyke groepe te deel -- jy eindig met presies dieselfde totale aantal klein groepe op enige manier, wat 18 groepe altesaam is. Om die vriendelikste faktorpaar te kies -- gewoonlik een met 2, 5, of 10 -- is wat hierdie metode werklik vinniger maak as om direk deur die volle 2-syfergetal te deel.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Mental division with remainders

source_trace: 1.1 Whole numbers Mental mathematics: Calculate quotients using knowledge of multiplication tables. Example: 84 ÷ 7 = 12, 66 ÷ 8 = 8 remainder 2
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 36, TERM 2 Grade 5, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Solve a division fact mentally using multiplication tables.
Recognise when a division does not divide exactly, and express the leftover amount as a remainder.
Use a known multiplication fact to quickly find a related division fact and its remainder.

english_content.narration_script: Let's try two mental division questions together. First, 84 divided by 7. Using your 7 times table, you know 7 times 12 equals 84, so 84 divided by 7 equals 12 exactly -- no leftovers. Now try 66 divided by 8. Using your 8 times table, the closest fact you know is 8 times 8 equals 64. That's close to 66, but not quite -- we're 2 short. So 66 divided by 8 equals 8, with 2 left over, which we write as '8 remainder 2'. Notice the strategy is exactly the same in both cases: think of the times table, find the closest fact, and if it doesn't land exactly, the gap becomes your remainder. This becomes especially useful once numbers get bigger and division by long methods gets slower -- mental estimation using multiplication facts you already know will always be faster, as long as you're comfortable finding remainders when a division doesn't come out perfectly even. Let's practise two more together. First, 45 divided by 9: recalling your 9 times table, 9 times 5 equals 45 exactly, so 45 divided by 9 equals 5, with no remainder at all. Now try 53 divided by 6: the closest fact you know is 6 times 8 equals 48. Since 53 is 5 more than 48, the answer is 8 remainder 5. Here's a useful check: a remainder must always be smaller than the number you're dividing by, since if it were equal to or bigger than the divisor, you could actually fit in one more whole group. In our example, the remainder 5 is smaller than the divisor 6, which confirms we've found the largest possible whole number of groups. This checking habit -- always confirming your remainder is smaller than your divisor -- is a quick way to catch mistakes before they slip through, and it's worth doing automatically every single time you calculate a division with a remainder, whether mentally or on paper. The stronger your times tables become through regular practice, the less thinking each of these checks will require -- eventually, spotting the closest multiplication fact and working out the remainder happens almost instantly, freeing up your attention for harder parts of a maths problem.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: 84 sweets splitting exactly into 12 rows of 7 with nothing left over.
66 sweets splitting into 8 rows of 8 with exactly 2 sweets left sitting outside the rows.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Kom ons probeer twee verstandelike delingsvrae saam. Eerste, 84 gedeel deur 7. Met jou 7-tafel weet jy 7 keer 12 is gelyk aan 84, so 84 gedeel deur 7 is gelyk aan 12 presies -- geen oorskot nie. Probeer nou 66 gedeel deur 8. Met jou 8-tafel is die naaste feit wat jy ken 8 keer 8 is gelyk aan 64. Dit is naby aan 66, maar nie heeltemal nie -- ons is 2 kort. So 66 gedeel deur 8 is gelyk aan 8, met 2 oor, wat ons skryf as '8 oor 2'. Let op die strategie is presies dieselfde in albei gevalle: dink aan die tafel, vind die naaste feit, en as dit nie presies land nie, word die gaping jou oorskot. Dit word veral nuttig sodra getalle groter word en deling met lang metodes stadiger word -- verstandelike beraming met vermenigvuldigingsfeite wat jy reeds ken sal altyd vinniger wees, solank jy gemaklik is om oorskotte te vind wanneer 'n deling nie presies eweredig uitkom nie. Kom ons oefen nog twee saam. Eerste, 45 gedeel deur 9: as jy jou 9-tafel onthou, is 9 keer 5 presies gelyk aan 45, so 45 gedeel deur 9 is gelyk aan 5, sonder enige oorskot. Probeer nou 53 gedeel deur 6: die naaste feit wat jy ken is 6 keer 8 is gelyk aan 48. Aangesien 53 5 meer as 48 is, is die antwoord 8 oor 5. Hier is 'n nuttige kontrole: 'n oorskot moet altyd kleiner as die getal wees waardeur jy deel, aangesien as dit gelyk aan of groter as die deler was, jy eintlik nog een volle groep sou kon inpas. In ons voorbeeld is die oorskot 5 kleiner as die deler 6, wat bevestig ons het die grootste moontlike heelgetal van groepe gevind. Hierdie kontrolegewoonte -- om altyd te bevestig jou oorskot is kleiner as jou deler -- is 'n vinnige manier om foute te vang voordat hulle deurglip, en dit is die moeite werd om outomaties elke enkele keer te doen as jy 'n deling met 'n oorskot bereken, of dit nou verstandelik of op papier is. Hoe sterker jou tafels deur gereelde oefening word, hoe minder dink elkeen van hierdie kontroles sal vereis -- uiteindelik gebeur om die naaste vermenigvuldigingsfeit raak te sien en die oorskot uit te werk amper onmiddellik, wat jou aandag vrymaak vir moeiliker dele van 'n wiskundeprobleem.

learning_objectives: Name the main skills grouped under this Grade 5 Whole Numbers section.
See how these Grade 5 skills build on the Grade 4 Whole Numbers unit.
Explain how this term's Grade 5 whole-numbers skills build on what was learned in Grade 4.

english_content.narration_script: This is the title heading for the Grade 5 Whole Numbers work this term, just like it was in Grade 4. Under this same heading, you'll find: division order still matters even with bigger numbers, dividing a 3-digit number by a 2-digit number using the factor method, mental division that sometimes leaves a remainder, and halving bigger 2- and 3-digit numbers. Notice the pattern: each of these is the exact same big idea from Grade 4, just applied to bigger, harder numbers. That's how maths tends to work year after year -- the core ideas don't disappear, they simply get stretched to handle more challenging numbers. Let's trace one of these skills through both grades to see exactly how it grows. In Grade 4, mental division using the times tables meant facts like 72 divided by 9 equals 8 -- always dividing exactly, with nothing left over. This year, in Grade 5, that same skill grows to include remainders: 66 divided by 8 equals 8, remainder 2, since 8 times 8 only gets you to 64, two short of 66. The underlying method hasn't changed at all -- you're still turning a division into a multiplication question you already know -- but now you also need to notice and record what's left over when the numbers don't divide perfectly. The same growth pattern happens with dividing by a 2-digit number instead of a 1-digit number, and with halving bigger numbers instead of smaller ones. This is exactly how the whole CAPS curriculum is designed: rather than throwing entirely new topics at you every year, most sections revisit last year's core idea and simply stretch it to handle bigger, messier numbers -- which is exactly why getting genuinely comfortable with a skill this year pays off again and again in the years that follow. It's worth pausing here to notice something encouraging: if last year's Whole Numbers work already feels comfortable to you, this year's version of the same skills, just with bigger numbers, should feel far less intimidating than it might first appear -- you're not starting from zero, you're simply stretching muscles you've already built.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Dit is die titelopskrif vir die Graad 5 Heelgetalle-werk vanjaar, net soos dit in Graad 4 was. Onder dieselfde opskrif sal jy vind: delingsvolgorde maak steeds saak selfs met groter getalle, om 'n 3-syfergetal deur 'n 2-syfergetal te deel met die faktormetode, verstandelike deling wat soms 'n oorskot laat, en halvering van groter 2- en 3-syfergetalle. Let op die patroon: elkeen van hierdie is presies dieselfde groot idee van Graad 4, net toegepas op groter, moeiliker getalle. Dit is hoe wiskunde geneig is om jaar na jaar te werk -- die kernidees verdwyn nie, hulle word bloot uitgerek om moeiliker getalle te hanteer. Kom ons spoor een van hierdie vaardighede deur albei grade om presies te sien hoe dit groei. In Graad 4 het verstandelike deling met die tafels feite soos 72 gedeel deur 9 is gelyk aan 8 beteken -- altyd presies deel, met niks oor nie. Vanjaar, in Graad 5, groei daardie selfde vaardigheid om oorskotte in te sluit: 66 gedeel deur 8 is gelyk aan 8, oor 2, aangesien 8 keer 8 jou net tot 64 bring, twee kort van 66. Die onderliggende metode het glad nie verander nie -- jy verander steeds 'n deling in 'n vermenigvuldigingsvraag wat jy reeds ken -- maar nou moet jy ook opmerk en aanteken wat oorbly wanneer die getalle nie perfek deel nie. Dieselfde groeipatroon gebeur met deling deur 'n 2-syfergetal in plaas van 'n 1-syfergetal, en met halvering van groter getalle in plaas van kleiner. Dit is presies hoe die hele CAPS-kurrikulum ontwerp is: eerder as om jou elke jaar met heeltemal nuwe onderwerpe te bestook, hersien die meeste afdelings verlede jaar se kernidee en rek dit eenvoudig uit om groter, deurmekaarder getalle te hanteer -- wat presies hoekom om werklik gemaklik te raak met 'n vaardigheid vanjaar weer en weer betaal in die jare wat volg. Dit is die moeite werd om hier te pouseer om iets bemoedigends op te merk: as verlede jaar se Heelgetalle-werk reeds gemaklik vir jou voel, behoort vanjaar se weergawe van dieselfde vaardighede, net met groter getalle, baie minder intimiderend te voel as wat dit aanvanklik mag lyk -- jy begin nie by nul nie, jy rek eenvoudig spiere wat jy reeds gebou het.

subject: Mathematics
topic_name: Division order matters (bigger numbers)

source_trace: 1.1 Whole numbers DIVISION Emphasize that numbers cannot be divided in any order. Example: 120 ÷ 10 ≠ 10 ÷ 120
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 36, TERM 2 Grade 5, content-outline table

learning_objectives: Confirm, with a new example, that division order still matters with bigger numbers.
Compare 120 ÷ 10 and 10 ÷ 120 to show they give different answers.
Determine, for a given division, whether swapping the order of the two numbers changes the answer.

english_content.narration_script: Let's check the division-order rule again, this time with bigger numbers. Take 120 divided by 10. That means 'how many groups of 10 fit into 120?' -- and the answer is 12. Now flip it: 10 divided by 120 means 'how many groups of 120 fit into 10?' -- and since 120 is much bigger than 10, the answer is a small fraction, nowhere near 12. So 120 divided by 10 is not equal to 10 divided by 120, exactly as we saw in Grade 4 with smaller numbers. No matter how big the numbers get, the order you divide in always matters. This is a rule that never changes as you move through the grades -- only the numbers involved get bigger and more challenging. Let's test the rule once more with 250 and 25. Calculate 250 divided by 25 first: how many 25s fit into 250? Exactly 10. Now flip it: 25 divided by 250 -- how many 250s fit into 25? Since 250 is far bigger than 25, not even one whole group fits, so the answer is a small fraction, nowhere near 10. So 250 divided by 25 does not equal 25 divided by 250 -- the correct way to write this is 250 ÷ 25 ≠ 25 ÷ 250, using the 'not equal to' symbol. It's worth asking: does this rule ever change once numbers get truly enormous, like thousands or millions? It doesn't -- the rule that division order matters has nothing to do with how big or small the numbers are; it's a fundamental property of division itself, true for every pair of numbers you'll ever divide, from the smallest single-digit sums to the largest numbers you'll meet in Senior Phase. Keep this rule firmly in mind as our numbers keep growing throughout the rest of this year. It's worth restating why this matters practically: whenever you're setting up a real-world division, like sharing money or splitting a group into teams, always double-check which number is the total amount being shared, and which is the number of groups -- getting that order backwards, even by accident, will give you a completely wrong, and sometimes nonsensical, answer.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A balance scale with '120 ÷ 10' settling to 12 on one side, and '10 ÷ 120' barely tipping on the other side.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Kom ons kontroleer die delingsvolgorde-reël weer, hierdie keer met groter getalle. Neem 120 gedeel deur 10. Dit beteken 'hoeveel groepe van 10 pas in 120?' -- en die antwoord is 12. Draai dit nou om: 10 gedeel deur 120 beteken 'hoeveel groepe van 120 pas in 10?' -- en aangesien 120 baie groter as 10 is, is die antwoord 'n klein breukdeel, glad nie naby 12 nie. So 120 gedeel deur 10 is nie gelyk aan 10 gedeel deur 120 nie, presies soos ons in Graad 4 met kleiner getalle gesien het. Maak nie saak hoe groot die getalle word nie, die volgorde waarin jy deel maak altyd saak. Dit is 'n reël wat nooit verander terwyl jy deur die grade beweeg nie -- net die betrokke getalle word groter en meer uitdagend. Kom ons toets die reël weer met 250 en 25. Bereken eers 250 gedeel deur 25: hoeveel 25's pas in 250? Presies 10. Draai dit nou om: 25 gedeel deur 250 -- hoeveel 250's pas in 25? Aangesien 250 baie groter as 25 is, pas nie eens een volle groep in nie, so die antwoord is 'n klein breukdeel, nêrens naby 10 nie. So 250 gedeel deur 25 is nie gelyk aan 25 gedeel deur 250 nie -- die korrekte manier om dit te skryf is 250 ÷ 25 ≠ 25 ÷ 250, met die 'nie gelyk aan'-simbool. Dit is die moeite werd om te vra: verander hierdie reël ooit sodra getalle werklik enorm word, soos duisende of miljoene? Dit verander nie -- die reël dat delingsvolgorde saak maak het niks te doen met hoe groot of klein die getalle is nie; dit is 'n fundamentele eienskap van deling self, waar vir elke paar getalle wat jy ooit sal deel, van die kleinste enkele-syfer-somme tot die grootste getalle wat jy in Senior Fase sal teëkom. Hou hierdie reël stewig in gedagte namate ons getalle regdeur die res van vanjaar aanhou groei. Dit is die moeite werd om te herhaal hoekom dit prakties saak maak: wanneer jy ook al 'n werklike deling opstel, soos geld deel of 'n groep in spanne verdeel, kontroleer altyd dubbel watter getal die totale bedrag is wat gedeel word, en watter die aantal groepe is -- om daardie volgorde omgekeerd te kry, selfs per ongeluk, sal jou 'n heeltemal verkeerde, en soms onsinnige, antwoord gee.
