subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Visual literacy: looking at the human body in action

source_trace: Observe and discuss visual stimuli in photographs and real objects to identify and name all art elements in images of the human body in action, and contrast.
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 50, Grade 4 Term 1 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Identify art elements (like shape, line, texture) in a photograph of the human body in action.
Identify examples of contrast in an image of the human body in action.
Apply this observation skill to your own artwork.

english_content.narration_script: Before we create our own art this term, let's train our eyes to really see what's already there. Look at a photograph or real object showing the human body in action -- maybe someone running, jumping, or dancing. Your job as a visual literacy detective is to identify and name all the art elements you can spot: shape (the outline of the body), line (the curves and angles it makes), texture, and more. Now let's look for something specific: contrast, which means a clear difference between two things -- light and dark, big and small, straight and curved. In a photo of the human body in action, you might notice contrast between a tense, straight leg and a relaxed, curved arm, or between light falling on one side of the body and shadow on the other. This kind of careful looking might feel like homework at first, but it's actually training your artist's eye -- because once you can spot contrast and other art elements in someone else's photograph, you'll start noticing exactly how to build the same qualities into your own drawings and models this term. Let's practise this eye-training with a second example: two art elements you could look for in any photograph, beyond contrast, are shape and texture. Shape means the outline or silhouette an object makes -- in our runner photo, the whole curved shape of the body mid-stride. Texture means how a surface looks like it would feel -- smooth skin, rough ground, soft flowing clothing. Once you've named shape, texture, and contrast in someone else's photograph, try the same exercise on a photo of yourself in action -- jumping, dancing, or playing sport. Notice how much more you see once you know exactly what to look for, compared to just glancing at the picture. This habit of naming what you see, rather than only reacting to whether an image 'looks nice', is genuinely the foundation of visual literacy, and it will make every drawing and model you create this term stronger, because you'll know exactly which qualities you're trying to capture. One last thought: try this same exercise on a photo from a magazine or a family album tonight, timing yourself to see how many art elements you can name in just one minute -- you'll likely surprise yourself with how much your eye has already learned to notice.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Voordat ons vanjaar ons eie kuns skep, kom ons oefen ons oë om regtig te sien wat reeds daar is. Kyk na 'n foto of regte voorwerp wat die menslike liggaam in aksie wys -- miskien iemand wat hardloop, spring, of dans. Jou taak as 'n visuele geletterdheid-speurder is om al die kunselemente wat jy kan raaksien te identifiseer en te noem: vorm (die omtrek van die liggaam), lyn (die krommings en hoeke wat dit maak), tekstuur, en meer. Kom ons kyk nou vir iets spesifieks: kontras, wat 'n duidelike verskil tussen twee dinge beteken -- lig en donker, groot en klein, reguit en gekrom. In 'n foto van die menslike liggaam in aksie mag jy kontras opmerk tussen 'n gespanne, reguit been en 'n ontspanne, gekromde arm, of tussen lig wat op een kant van die liggaam val en skaduwee op die ander. Hierdie soort noukeurige kyk mag aanvanklik soos huiswerk voel, maar dit oefen eintlik jou kunstenaarsoog -- want sodra jy kontras en ander kunselemente in iemand anders se foto kan raaksien, sal jy presies begin opmerk hoe om dieselfde eienskappe in jou eie tekeninge en modelle vanjaar in te bou. Kom ons oefen hierdie oog-opleiding met 'n tweede voorbeeld: twee kunselemente wat jy in enige foto kan soek, buiten kontras, is vorm en tekstuur. Vorm beteken die omtrek of silhoeët wat 'n voorwerp maak -- in ons hardloper-foto, die hele gekromde vorm van die liggaam middel-tree. Tekstuur beteken hoe 'n oppervlak lyk asof dit sou voel -- gladde vel, growwe grond, sagte vloeiende klere. Sodra jy vorm, tekstuur, en kontras in iemand anders se foto genoem het, probeer dieselfde oefening op 'n foto van jouself in aksie -- spring, dans, of sport speel. Let op hoeveel meer jy sien sodra jy presies weet waarna om te kyk, vergeleke met net na die prentjie kyk. Hierdie gewoonte om te noem wat jy sien, eerder as om net te reageer op of 'n beeld 'mooi lyk', is werklik die grondslag van visuele geletterdheid, en dit sal elke tekening en model wat jy vanjaar skep sterker maak, want jy sal presies weet watter eienskappe jy probeer vaslê. Een laaste gedagte: probeer hierdie selfde oefening vanaand op 'n foto uit 'n tydskrif of 'n familiealbum, en tydsberekening jouself om te sien hoeveel kunselemente jy in net een minuut kan noem -- jy sal jouself waarskynlik verras met hoeveel jou oog reeds geleer het om raak te sien.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Create in 2D: images of family and friends

source_trace: Drawing and/or colour media: exploring a variety of media and techniques. Art elements: secondary colour used in own images of self and others. Design principles: contrast used in own images of self a
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 50, Grade 4 Term 1 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Use a variety of drawing and colour media (pencils, charcoal, inks, oil pastels, paint) to create an image.
Use secondary colours (orange, green, purple) in an image of yourself and others.
Use contrast deliberately in your own image of family and friends.

english_content.narration_script: This term's project is to create a two-dimensional image of family and friends, and you'll have real freedom in how you make it, using materials like 2B or 3B pencils, charcoal, coloured inks, oil pastels, or tempera paint. Part of this term's challenge is exploring how each of these media behaves differently -- charcoal smudges softly, while ink stays sharp and bold. Let's focus on two specific skills this term. First, secondary colours: remember that mixing two primary colours creates a secondary colour -- red and yellow make orange, yellow and blue make green, and blue and red make purple. Try deliberately using these secondary colours somewhere in your image of family or friends, rather than only primary colours. Second, contrast: think about creating a clear difference somewhere in your image -- maybe a light figure against a dark background, or a big figure next to a small one. As you draw people you know and care about, try to actually see them: their poses, their expressions, their relationships to each other -- rather than drawing a generic figure. The goal isn't a 'perfect' picture; it's genuinely exploring colour, contrast, and your own way of representing the people who matter to you. Let's revisit the secondary colours one more time, since knowing all three matters, not just green. Red and yellow make orange, yellow and blue make green, and blue and red make purple -- and it's worth noticing that each secondary colour sits directly between its two 'parent' primary colours, which is exactly why mixing them feels so natural. As you plan your family and friends drawing, think about how you could use these colours meaningfully -- maybe a favourite orange jumper someone actually wears, or a purple flower in the background of your scene, rather than choosing colours randomly. Combine this with contrast: perhaps your orange jumper stands out clearly against a cooler purple or green background, using both of this term's new ideas together in one deliberate choice. Real family photos are full of exactly these kinds of small, specific details -- a particular piece of clothing, a certain expression, a familiar background -- and noticing them is what will make your drawing feel like it's truly about your own family and friends, not a generic group of people.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vanjaar se projek is om 'n tweedimensionele beeld van familie en vriende te skep, en jy sal regte vryheid hê in hoe jy dit maak, met materiale soos 2B- of 3B-potlode, houtskool, gekleurde inkte, olie-pastelle, of tempera-verf. Deel van hierdie kwartaal se uitdaging is om te ondersoek hoe elkeen van hierdie media anders optree -- houtskool vee sag uit, terwyl ink skerp en vet bly. Kom ons fokus op twee spesifieke vaardighede vanjaar. Eerste, sekondêre kleure: onthou dat die meng van twee primêre kleure 'n sekondêre kleur skep -- rooi en geel maak oranje, geel en blou maak groen, en blou en rooi maak pers. Probeer doelbewus hierdie sekondêre kleure êrens in jou beeld van familie of vriende gebruik, eerder as net primêre kleure. Tweede, kontras: dink aan die skep van 'n duidelike verskil êrens in jou beeld -- miskien 'n ligte figuur teen 'n donker agtergrond, of 'n groot figuur langs 'n klein een. Terwyl jy mense teken wat jy ken en omgee, probeer om hulle regtig te sien: hul houdings, hul uitdrukkings, hul verhoudings met mekaar -- eerder as om 'n generiese figuur te teken. Die doel is nie 'n 'perfekte' prentjie nie; dit is om regtig kleur, kontras, en jou eie manier om die mense wat vir jou saak maak voor te stel, te verken. Kom ons besoek weer die sekondêre kleure, aangesien om al drie te ken saak maak, nie net groen nie. Rooi en geel maak oranje, geel en blou maak groen, en blou en rooi maak pers -- en dit is die moeite werd om op te let elke sekondêre kleur sit direk tussen sy twee 'ouer' primêre kleure, wat presies hoekom om hulle te meng so natuurlik voel. Terwyl jy jou familie-en-vriende-tekening beplan, dink oor hoe jy hierdie kleure betekenisvol kan gebruik -- miskien 'n gunsteling oranje trui wat iemand werklik dra, of 'n pers blom in die agtergrond van jou toneel, eerder as om kleure lukraak te kies. Kombineer dit met kontras: miskien staan jou oranje trui duidelik uit teen 'n koeler pers of groen agtergrond, en gebruik beide vanjaar se nuwe idees saam in een doelbewuste keuse. Regte familiefoto's is vol presies hierdie soort klein, spesifieke besonderhede -- 'n spesifieke stuk klere, 'n sekere uitdrukking, 'n bekende agtergrond -- en om hulle raak te sien is wat jou tekening werklik oor jou eie familie en vriende sal laat voel, nie 'n generiese groep mense nie.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Create in 3D: modelling self and others

source_trace: Skills and techniques: earthenware clay. Art elements: texture, shape/form used in own models of human figure. Design principles: use and naming of contrast. Spatial awareness: use of space (front, ba
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 50, Grade 4 Term 1 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Use earthenware clay skills and techniques to model a human figure.
Use texture and shape/form deliberately in your own model.
Show spatial awareness by making sure your model looks good from the front, back, and sides.

english_content.narration_script: This term, we move from flat drawing into three-dimensional sculpture, using earthenware clay to model the human figure -- yourself or someone else. Clay lets you explore two art elements in a very physical way: texture, the surface quality of your model (smooth, rough, bumpy), and shape or form, the overall three-dimensional structure your figure takes. As you model, think deliberately about contrast: perhaps a smooth face against a textured piece of clothing, or a large body shape balanced by small, delicate hands. Here's something that makes 3D art genuinely different from a drawing: spatial awareness. A drawing only has one view, but your clay model exists in real space, which means it needs to look complete and considered from the front, the back, and both sides -- not just from whichever angle you happened to be looking at while you made it. Get in the habit of turning your model around regularly as you work, checking every side, rather than only focusing on the view facing you. And remember, appropriate use of tools matters too -- using your clay tools correctly and safely is part of building real skill with this material. Let's think a little more about the tool-use point, since it matters beyond just following a rule. Clay tools like wire loops, wooden modelling tools, and simple carving tools each do a specific job -- a wire loop removes clay smoothly to shape a form, while a fine tool can add small details like fingers or facial features. Using the wrong tool, or using a tool carelessly, can damage your model or even hurt you, which is exactly why appropriate use matters for both safety and quality. As you build your figure, alternate between adding clay (to build up shape) and removing clay (to refine details), checking texture and form as you go rather than only at the very end. And remember your earlier visual literacy training: look for contrast in your own figure as you shape it, just as you practised spotting it in photographs -- a smooth face against roughly textured hair is a small, deliberate choice that will make your finished model noticeably more interesting to look at from every angle.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vanjaar beweeg ons van plat tekeninge na driedimensionele beeldhouwerk, deur erdewerk-klei te gebruik om die menslike figuur te modelleer -- jouself of iemand anders. Klei laat jou toe om twee kunselemente op 'n baie fisiese manier te verken: tekstuur, die oppervlakkwaliteit van jou model (glad, growwig, hobbelrig), en vorm, die algehele driedimensionele struktuur wat jou figuur aanneem. Terwyl jy modelleer, dink doelbewus aan kontras: miskien 'n gladde gesig teen 'n gestruktureerde stuk klere, of 'n groot liggaamsvorm gebalanseer deur klein, delikate hande. Hier is iets wat 3D-kuns werklik anders as 'n tekening maak: ruimtelike bewustheid. 'n Tekening het net een aansig, maar jou kleimodel bestaan in werklike ruimte, wat beteken dit moet volledig en oorwoë lyk van voor, van agter, en van albei kante -- nie net van watter hoek jy toevallig gekyk het terwyl jy dit gemaak het nie. Maak dit gewoonte om jou model gereeld om te draai terwyl jy werk, elke kant te kontroleer, eerder as om net op die aansig voor jou te fokus. En onthou, toepaslike gebruik van gereedskap is ook belangrik -- om jou kleigereedskap korrek en veilig te gebruik is deel van die bou van regte vaardigheid met hierdie materiaal. Kom ons dink 'n bietjie meer oor die gereedskapgebruik-punt, aangesien dit meer as net 'n reël volg beteken. Kleigereedskap soos drooglusse, houtmodelleringsgereedskap, en eenvoudige kerfgereedskap doen elkeen 'n spesifieke werk -- 'n drooglus verwyder klei glad om 'n vorm te vorm, terwyl 'n fyn gereedskap klein besonderhede soos vingers of gesigskenmerke kan byvoeg. Om die verkeerde gereedskap te gebruik, of gereedskap onversigtig te gebruik, kan jou model beskadig of jou selfs seermaak, wat presies hoekom toepaslike gebruik vir beide veiligheid en kwaliteit saak maak. Terwyl jy jou figuur bou, wissel tussen klei byvoeg (om vorm op te bou) en klei verwyder (om besonderhede te verfyn), en kontroleer tekstuur en vorm terwyl jy gaan eerder as net heel aan die einde. En onthou jou vroeëre visuele geletterdheid-opleiding: soek kontras in jou eie figuur terwyl jy dit vorm, net soos jy geoefen het om dit in foto's te raaksien -- 'n gladde gesig teen growwig-getekstuurde hare is 'n klein, doelbewuste keuse wat jou voltooide model merkbaar interessanter sal laat lyk van elke hoek.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Visual literacy: lettering and pattern-making

source_trace: Observe and discuss visual stimuli to identify and name all art elements, contrast and proportion in lettering and/or pattern-making.
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 50, Grade 4 Term 2 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Identify art elements in examples of lettering and pattern-making.
Identify contrast and proportion in lettering and pattern-making.
Apply this observation skill to your own work.

english_content.narration_script: This term, our visual literacy focus shifts to lettering and pattern-making. Look closely at examples -- posters, book covers, decorative borders -- and identify the art elements at work: line, shape, and colour used to form letters or repeating patterns. Now look for two specific qualities: contrast (a clear difference, like a bold letter against a plain background) and proportion (how the size of one part relates to another, like a tall letter next to a short one, or a large pattern shape next to a small one). Ask deeper questions as you look: why did the designer choose that particular contrast? Does the proportion feel balanced, or deliberately unbalanced for effect? This close observation directly prepares you for your own lettering and pattern-making project this term -- once you can name what makes an existing design work, you can start making those same deliberate choices yourself. Let's dig a little deeper into how contrast and proportion work together in lettering specifically. Imagine a poster where the title is written in huge, bold letters, while a small line of extra information sits underneath in thin, plain text -- the size difference is proportion, since the two pieces of text relate to each other in scale, but the bold-versus-plain difference is contrast. Designers use this pairing constantly, because it tells your eye exactly where to look first (the big bold title) and what to read second (the smaller details). Try finding this same pairing in packaging at home, a school notice, or even a book cover -- once you know to look for it, you'll start noticing it everywhere. This kind of observation is what separates simply liking a design from actually understanding why it works, which is exactly the skill this term's lettering and pattern-making project will ask you to put into practice yourself. Try applying this same two-question habit -- what's the contrast, and what's the proportion -- to a road sign or a shop sign you see on your way home today. You'll likely find both qualities at work even in the simplest, most functional designs, not just in posters made purely for decoration.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A decorative lettering poster with 'contrast' and 'proportion' labels pointing to specific letters and pattern shapes.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vanjaar skuif ons visuele geletterdheid-fokus na skryfwerk en patroonmaak. Kyk noukeurig na voorbeelde -- plakkate, boekomslae, dekoratiewe grense -- en identifiseer die kunselemente aan die werk: lyn, vorm, en kleur gebruik om letters of herhalende patrone te vorm. Kyk nou vir twee spesifieke eienskappe: kontras ('n duidelike verskil, soos 'n vetgedrukte letter teen 'n plein agtergrond) en proporsie (hoe die grootte van een deel met 'n ander verband hou, soos 'n lang letter langs 'n kort een, of 'n groot patroonvorm langs 'n klein een). Vra dieper vrae terwyl jy kyk: hoekom het die ontwerper daardie spesifieke kontras gekies? Voel die proporsie gebalanseerd, of doelbewus ongebalanseerd vir effek? Hierdie noukeurige waarneming berei jou direk voor vir jou eie skryfwerk- en patroonmaakprojek vanjaar -- sodra jy kan noem wat 'n bestaande ontwerp laat werk, kan jy begin om dieselfde doelbewuste keuses self te maak. Kom ons delf 'n bietjie dieper in hoe kontras en proporsie saam in skryfwerk spesifiek werk. Stel jou 'n plakkaat voor waar die titel in enorme, vetgedrukte letters geskryf is, terwyl 'n klein reël ekstra inligting daaronder in dun, plein teks sit -- die grootteverskil is proporsie, aangesien die twee stukke teks in skaal met mekaar verband hou, maar die vetgedruk-teenoor-plein-verskil is kontras. Ontwerpers gebruik hierdie paring voortdurend, want dit vertel jou oog presies waarheen om eerste te kyk (die groot vetgedrukte titel) en wat om tweede te lees (die kleiner besonderhede). Probeer hierdie selfde paring in verpakking by die huis, 'n skoolkennisgewing, of selfs 'n boekomslag vind -- sodra jy weet om daarna te soek, sal jy dit orals begin raaksien. Hierdie soort waarneming is wat om eenvoudig van 'n ontwerp te hou skei van om werklik te verstaan hoekom dit werk, wat presies die vaardigheid is wat vanjaar se skryfwerk- en patroonmaakprojek jou sal vra om self in praktyk te bring. Probeer hierdie selfde twee-vraag-gewoonte -- wat is die kontras, en wat is die proporsie -- toepas op 'n padteken of 'n winkelteken wat jy vandag op pad huis toe sien. Jy sal waarskynlik albei eienskappe aan die werk vind selfs in die eenvoudigste, mees funksionele ontwerpe, nie net in plakkate suiwer vir dekorasie gemaak nie.

The visual difference between bold and plain also shows contrast.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Create in 2D: creative lettering and pattern-making

source_trace: Drawing and/or colour media exploring a variety of media and techniques. Art elements: line, shape, colour used in own lettering/pattern-making; drawing, cutting and sticking shapes in series. Design
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 50, Grade 4 Term 2 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Use line, shape, and colour to create your own lettering or pattern.
Practise drawing, cutting, and sticking shapes in a series to form a pattern.
Use contrast deliberately in the shapes and sizes of your lettering or pattern.

english_content.narration_script: This term you'll design and create your own lettering or pattern, using pencils, charcoal, coloured inks, oil pastels, or tempera paint. Start by exploring line, shape, and colour: what kind of letter shapes do you want to draw? What colours will make them stand out? A useful technique here is drawing, cutting, and sticking shapes in a series -- creating one shape, then repeating and arranging it to build a full pattern, rather than drawing everything freehand each time. As you build your design, use contrast deliberately: vary the shapes and sizes within your pattern or lettering, so some parts are bold and large while others are smaller and quieter, creating visual interest rather than one flat, repetitive look. This project is a great chance to notice how graphic designers use exactly these same tools -- line, shape, colour, repetition, and contrast -- to make posters, logos, and patterns that catch our eye every day. Let's think through why graphic designers rely on exactly these tools -- line, shape, colour, repetition, and contrast -- in their everyday work, since it's a genuinely useful question to sit with. A shop logo, a road sign, or a cereal box all need to communicate something instantly, often to someone who only glances at them for a second, which means every visual choice has to work hard: a repeated shape can make a brand instantly recognisable, and strong contrast can make important information visible even from a distance. As you build your own pattern this term, imagine your design needs to be recognised quickly, the way a real logo does -- does your repeating shape read clearly even at a glance, or does it need simplifying? Testing your design this way, by imagining a stranger seeing it for just a second, is exactly the kind of thinking that separates a decorative doodle from genuine graphic design. As a final check before you call your pattern finished, hold it at arm's length or pin it to a wall and step back several paces -- design choices that seemed clear up close sometimes disappear from a normal viewing distance, and this simple test often reveals exactly where a little more contrast or a bolder repeated shape is still needed.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A hand cutting out repeated shapes and arranging them into a pattern, some bold and large, others small.
visual_storyboard.on_screen_text: Cutting and arranging shapes in a series

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vanjaar sal jy jou eie skryfwerk of patroon ontwerp en skep, met potlode, houtskool, gekleurde inkte, olie-pastelle, of tempera-verf. Begin deur lyn, vorm, en kleur te verken: watter soort lettervorms wil jy teken? Watter kleure sal hulle laat uitstaan? 'n Nuttige tegniek hier is om vorms in 'n reeks te teken, te sny, en te plak -- om een vorm te skep, dan te herhaal en te rangskik om 'n volledige patroon te bou, eerder as om elke keer alles vryhand te teken. Terwyl jy jou ontwerp bou, gebruik kontras doelbewus: wissel die vorms en groottes binne jou patroon of skryfwerk, sodat sommige dele vetgedruk en groot is terwyl ander kleiner en stiller is, wat visuele belangstelling skep eerder as een plat, herhalende voorkoms. Hierdie projek is 'n goeie geleentheid om op te merk hoe grafiese ontwerpers presies dieselfde gereedskap gebruik -- lyn, vorm, kleur, herhaling, en kontras -- om plakkate, logo's, en patrone te maak wat elke dag ons oog vang. Kom ons dink deur hoekom grafiese ontwerpers presies op hierdie gereedskap staatmaak -- lyn, vorm, kleur, herhaling, en kontras -- in hul alledaagse werk, aangesien dit 'n werklik nuttige vraag is om by stil te staan. 'n Winkellogo, 'n padteken, of 'n graankosboks moet almal iets onmiddellik kommunikeer, dikwels aan iemand wat net vir 'n sekonde daarna kyk, wat beteken elke visuele keuse moet hard werk: 'n herhaalde vorm kan 'n handelsmerk onmiddellik herkenbaar maak, en sterk kontras kan belangrike inligting selfs van 'n afstand sigbaar maak. Terwyl jy jou eie patroon vanjaar bou, verbeel jou ontwerp moet vinnig herken word, soos 'n regte logo doen -- lees jou herhalende vorm duidelik selfs met 'n oogopslag, of moet dit vereenvoudig word? Om jou ontwerp so te toets, deur jou 'n vreemdeling voor te stel wat dit net vir 'n sekonde sien, is presies die soort denke wat 'n dekoratiewe krabbel van ware grafiese ontwerp skei. As 'n finale kontrole voordat jy jou patroon voltooid verklaar, hou dit op armlengte of speld dit teen 'n muur en tree verskeie treë terug -- ontwerpkeuses wat van naby duidelik gelyk het verdwyn soms van 'n gewone besigtigingsafstand, en hierdie eenvoudige toets openbaar dikwels presies waar 'n bietjie meer kontras of 'n vetgedrukter herhalende vorm nog nodig is.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Create in 3D: mobiles or stabiles

source_trace: Recyclable materials. Skills: pasting, cutting, wrapping, tying, joining. Art elements: texture, shape/form. Design principles: introduce proportion. Spatial awareness: use of space, appropriate use o
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 50, Grade 4 Term 2 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Use recyclable materials and joining techniques (pasting, cutting, wrapping, tying) to construct a mobile or stabile.
Use texture and shape/form deliberately in your construction.
Use proportion by relating the size of one part of your mobile to another.

english_content.narration_script: This term's 3D project uses recyclable materials -- cardboard off-cuts, beads, sequins, ribbon, natural objects, cotton, and wire -- to build a mobile (a hanging construction that moves) or a stabile (a similar construction that stands still). You'll practise real joining skills: pasting, cutting, wrapping, tying, and joining different materials together securely. As you build, think about texture and shape or form: mixing rough cardboard with smooth ribbon, or round beads with angular cut shapes. This term also introduces a new design principle: proportion, specifically the size of one form in relation to another -- if one hanging shape is huge and another tiny, how does that balance (or intentionally unbalance) your whole construction? Since a mobile or stabile exists in real space, keep spatial awareness in mind too: consider the front, back, and sides of the objects you're building, not just one flat view. And always use your tools appropriately and safely -- good technique with scissors, glue, and wire is a real skill you're building here, not just a safety rule. Let's think a bit more about proportion in a hanging construction, since it behaves a little differently from proportion in a flat drawing. On a mobile, each hanging piece needs to balance not just visually but often physically too -- if one shape is much heavier than the others, the whole mobile might tip or hang unevenly, which means proportion here connects directly to real physics, not just appearance. This is a great opportunity to experiment: try hanging pieces of very different sizes and see what actually happens when you let the whole thing swing freely, then adjust the string lengths or piece sizes until it hangs the way you want. A stabile doesn't face this exact challenge since it stands rather than hangs, but it still needs a stable base relative to its height, or it will simply topple over. In both cases, this term's project teaches a lesson that goes beyond art class: sometimes a design choice isn't just about how something looks, but about whether it will actually work in the real world. Before you call your mobile or stabile finished, test it one last time exactly as it will actually be seen or used -- hang it where it will really hang, or stand it where it will really stand -- since a construction that looks perfect lying flat on a table can behave completely differently once gravity and real space are involved.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A collection of recyclable materials (cardboard, beads, ribbon, wire) being pasted, cut, wrapped and tied into a hanging mobile.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vanjaar se 3D-projek gebruik herwinbare materiale -- kartonafsnitte, krale, flenters, lint, natuurlike voorwerpe, katoen, en draad -- om 'n mobile ('n hangende konstruksie wat beweeg) of 'n stabile ('n soortgelyke konstruksie wat stil staan) te bou. Jy sal regte saamvoegvaardighede oefen: plak, sny, toedraai, vasknoop, en verskillende materiale veilig aan mekaar verbind. Terwyl jy bou, dink aan tekstuur en vorm: growwe karton meng met gladde lint, of ronde krale met hoekige gesnyde vorms. Vanjaar stel ook 'n nuwe ontwerpbeginsel bekend: proporsie, spesifiek die grootte van een vorm in verhouding tot 'n ander -- as een hangende vorm enorm is en 'n ander piepklein, hoe balanseer (of ontbalanseer doelbewus) dit jou hele konstruksie? Aangesien 'n mobile of stabile in werklike ruimte bestaan, hou ook ruimtelike bewustheid in gedagte: oorweeg die voor-, agter-, en kante van die voorwerpe wat jy bou, nie net een plat aansig nie. En gebruik altyd jou gereedskap toepaslik en veilig -- goeie tegniek met skêre, gom, en draad is 'n regte vaardigheid wat jy hier bou, nie net 'n veiligheidsreël nie. Kom ons dink 'n bietjie meer oor proporsie in 'n hangende konstruksie, aangesien dit effens anders as proporsie in 'n plat tekening gedra. Op 'n mobile moet elke hangende stuk nie net visueel balanseer nie, maar dikwels ook fisies -- as een vorm baie swaarder as die ander is, mag die hele mobile kantel of ongelyk hang, wat beteken proporsie hier direk met werklike fisika verband hou, nie net voorkoms nie. Dit is 'n goeie geleentheid om te eksperimenteer: probeer stukke van baie verskillende groottes ophang en sien wat werklik gebeur wanneer jy die hele ding vrylik laat swaai, pas dan die toulengtes of stukgroottes aan totdat dit hang soos jy wil hê. 'n Stabile staar nie hierdie presiese uitdaging in die gesig nie aangesien dit staan eerder as hang, maar dit het steeds 'n stabiele basis relatief tot sy hoogte nodig, of dit sal eenvoudig omval. In albei gevalle leer vanjaar se projek 'n les wat verder as kunsklas gaan: soms gaan 'n ontwerpkeuse nie net oor hoe iets lyk nie, maar oor of dit werklik in die werklike wêreld sal werk. Voordat jy jou mobile of stabile voltooid verklaar, toets dit een laaste keer presies soos dit werklik gesien of gebruik sal word -- hang dit waar dit werklik sal hang, of laat dit staan waar dit werklik sal staan -- aangesien 'n konstruksie wat perfek lyk plat op 'n tafel heeltemal anders kan gedra sodra swaartekrag en werklike ruimte betrokke is.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Visual literacy: images of wild and domestic animals

source_trace: Observe and discuss visual stimuli to identify all art elements, contrast and proportion in images of wild and domestic animals.
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 51, Grade 4 Term 3 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Identify art elements in photographs and artworks of wild or domestic animals.
Identify contrast and proportion in images of animals.
Apply this observation skill to your own animal artwork.

english_content.narration_script: This term, our visual literacy focus is wild and domestic animals. Look at photographs, artworks, and real objects showing animals, and identify the art elements present: shape (the animal's outline), texture (fur, feathers, scales), and colour. Now look specifically for contrast and proportion. Contrast might appear as a striped pattern (dark against light), or a small kitten beside a large dog. Proportion is about size relationships -- notice how an animal's head, body, and legs relate to each other in size, since getting these proportions right (or deliberately wrong, for a cartoon effect) changes how believable or stylised an animal image looks. Ask yourself deeper questions: how did the artist use texture to show whether an animal's coat looks soft or rough? These are exactly the observations that will help you create convincing, expressive images of animals in your own 2D and 3D work this term. Let's think a bit further about how getting proportions 'wrong' on purpose actually works as an artistic choice. A cartoon puppy might have an oversized head and huge eyes compared to its tiny body -- proportions that would look strange in a realistic drawing, but that make the puppy feel instantly appealing and expressive in a cartoon style. This shows something important: proportion isn't just about being 'accurate', it's a tool an artist chooses to use deliberately, depending on the effect they want. A realistic animal drawing calls for careful, accurate proportions, while a playful cartoon calls for exaggerated ones. As you study photographs of animals this term, try sketching the same animal twice: once trying for realistic proportions, and once deliberately exaggerating them for a cartoon effect. Comparing your two attempts side by side is a great way to really understand what proportion is actually doing in each style. Try this exercise tonight with a family pet, or a photo of one: spend a full minute just looking before naming a single art element, then see how many of shape, texture, colour, contrast, and proportion you can genuinely spot once you've really taken the time to look closely. Keep this one-minute habit going with a different animal every day this week, and notice how much faster your eye starts finding these qualities each time.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A photograph of a wild animal (e.g. a zebra) with labels pointing to texture (stripes), shape, and proportion (leg to body size).

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vanjaar is ons visuele geletterdheid-fokus wilde en mak diere. Kyk na foto's, kunswerke, en regte voorwerpe wat diere wys, en identifiseer die kunselemente teenwoordig: vorm (die dier se omtrek), tekstuur (pels, vere, skubbe), en kleur. Kyk nou spesifiek vir kontras en proporsie. Kontras mag verskyn as 'n gestreepte patroon (donker teen lig), of 'n klein katjie langs 'n groot hond. Proporsie gaan oor groottewaarhoudinge -- let op hoe 'n dier se kop, liggaam, en pote in grootte met mekaar verband hou, aangesien hierdie proporsies reg kry (of doelbewus verkeerd, vir 'n spotprenteffek) verander hoe geloofwaardig of gestileer 'n dierebeeld lyk. Vra jouself dieper vrae: hoe het die kunstenaar tekstuur gebruik om te wys of 'n dier se pels sag of grof lyk? Dit is presies die waarnemings wat jou sal help om oortuigende, uitdrukkingsvolle beelde van diere in jou eie 2D- en 3D-werk vanjaar te skep. Kom ons dink 'n bietjie verder oor hoe om proporsies doelbewus 'verkeerd' te kry eintlik as 'n kunssinnige keuse werk. 'n Spotprent-hondjie mag 'n oorgrootte kop en enorme oë hê vergeleke met sy piepklein liggaam -- proporsies wat vreemd sou lyk in 'n realistiese tekening, maar wat die hondjie onmiddellik aantreklik en uitdrukkingsvol in 'n spotprentstyl laat voel. Dit wys iets belangriks: proporsie gaan nie net oor 'akkuraat' wees nie, dit is 'n gereedskap wat 'n kunstenaar doelbewus kies om te gebruik, afhangende van die effek wat hulle wil hê. 'n Realistiese diertekening vra vir noukeurige, akkurate proporsies, terwyl 'n speelse spotprent vir oordrewe s'n vra. Terwyl jy vanjaar foto's van diere bestudeer, probeer dieselfde dier twee keer skets: een keer probeer vir realistiese proporsies, en een keer dit doelbewus oordryf vir 'n spotprenteffek. Om jou twee pogings langs mekaar te vergelyk is 'n uitstekende manier om werklik te verstaan wat proporsie in elke styl eintlik doen. Probeer hierdie oefening vanaand met 'n gesinstroeteldier, of 'n foto van een: spandeer 'n volle minuut net om te kyk voordat jy een enkele kunselement noem, en kyk dan hoeveel van vorm, tekstuur, kleur, kontras, en proporsie jy werklik kan raaksien sodra jy regtig die tyd geneem het om noukeurig te kyk. Hou hierdie een-minuut-gewoonte elke dag hierdie week met 'n ander dier aan die gang, en let op hoeveel vinniger jou oog hierdie eienskappe elke keer begin vind.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Create in 2D: wild or domestic animals in their environment

source_trace: Drawing and/or colour media exploring techniques. Art elements: use related colour. Design principles: reinforce contrast and proportion.
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 51, Grade 4 Term 3 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Create a 2D image of a wild or domestic animal in its environment.
Use related colours (colours near each other on the colour wheel) in your image.
Reinforce your use of contrast and proportion from earlier observation practice.

english_content.narration_script: This term's drawing project is a wild or domestic animal in its own environment -- a lion in the savannah, a dog in a garden, a fish in the sea. This term introduces related colour: colours that sit near each other on the colour wheel, like blues and greens, or oranges and reds, which naturally look harmonious together. Try using related colours to paint your animal and its environment as one connected, believable scene, rather than clashing, unrelated colours. This is also your chance to reinforce contrast and proportion, the same qualities you practised observing in other images: make sure your animal's body proportions look convincing, and use contrast (perhaps a bright animal against a duller background) to make your subject stand out. Take your time observing your chosen animal, even from a photograph, before you start drawing -- the more carefully you look, the more convincing your final image will be. Let's take the related colour idea a little further by thinking about a different environment -- a lion in the savannah. Related colours here might be yellows, oranges, and warm browns, since they sit close together on the colour wheel and naturally suggest dry grass and warm sunlight. Notice how choosing related colours for a specific environment isn't just a rule to follow -- it's a genuine observation about the real world: a fish's underwater world really is dominated by blues and greens, and a savannah really is dominated by warm yellows and browns, so using related colours in these scenes isn't only harmonious, it's also more accurate. As you plan your own animal-in-environment drawing, take a moment before you start to decide: what family of related colours actually matches the real environment you're depicting, and how can you use contrast within that same colour family to still make your animal stand out clearly? Before you begin painting, it can help to gather two or three reference images of your chosen environment, checking whether the colours you plan to use genuinely match what's actually there -- real environments are often more subtly coloured than we remember them, and a quick reference check can save you from an inaccurate first impression.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A colour wheel highlighting a 'related colours' section (e.g. blues through greens), then a drawing of an animal in its environment using those related colours.
visual_storyboard.on_screen_text: Related colours: harmony in one scene

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vanjaar se tekenprojek is 'n wilde of mak dier in sy eie omgewing -- 'n leeu in die savanne, 'n hond in 'n tuin, 'n vis in die see. Vanjaar stel verwante kleur bekend: kleure wat naby mekaar op die kleurwiel sit, soos blou en groen, of oranje en rooi, wat natuurlik harmonies saam lyk. Probeer verwante kleure gebruik om jou dier en sy omgewing as een verbonde, geloofwaardige toneel te verf, eerder as botsende, onverwante kleure. Dit is ook jou kans om kontras en proporsie te versterk, dieselfde eienskappe wat jy in ander beelde geoefen het om waar te neem: maak seker jou dier se liggaamsproporsies lyk oortuigend, en gebruik kontras (miskien 'n helder dier teen 'n dowwer agtergrond) om jou onderwerp te laat uitstaan. Neem jou tyd om jou gekose dier waar te neem, selfs van 'n foto af, voordat jy begin teken -- hoe noukeuriger jy kyk, hoe oortuigender jou finale beeld sal wees. Kom ons neem die verwante-kleur-idee 'n bietjie verder deur oor 'n ander omgewing te dink -- 'n leeu in die savanne. Verwante kleure hier mag gelerig, oranjerig, en warm bruin wees, aangesien hulle naby mekaar op die kleurwiel sit en natuurlik droë gras en warm sonlig voorstel. Let op hoe om verwante kleure vir 'n spesifieke omgewing te kies nie net 'n reël is om te volg nie -- dit is 'n ware waarneming oor die werklike wêreld: 'n vis se onderwaterwêreld word werklik deur blou en groen oorheers, en 'n savanne word werklik deur warm geel en bruin oorheers, so om verwante kleure in hierdie tonele te gebruik is nie net harmonieus nie, dit is ook meer akkuraat. Terwyl jy jou eie dier-in-omgewing-tekening beplan, neem 'n oomblik voordat jy begin om te besluit: watter familie van verwante kleure pas werklik by die werklike omgewing wat jy uitbeeld, en hoe kan jy kontras binne daardie selfde kleurfamilie gebruik om jou dier steeds duidelik te laat uitstaan? Voordat jy begin verf, kan dit help om twee of drie verwysingsbeelde van jou gekose omgewing te versamel, en te kontroleer of die kleure wat jy beplan om te gebruik werklik ooreenstem met wat werklik daar is -- werklike omgewings is dikwels meer subtiel gekleur as wat ons hulle onthou, en 'n vinnige verwysingskontrole kan jou van 'n onakkurate eerste indruk red.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: 'n Kleurwiel lig 'n 'verwante kleure'-afdeling uit (bv. blou deur groen), dan 'n tekening van 'n dier in sy omgewing wat daardie verwante kleure gebruik.
visual_storyboard.on_screen_text: Verwante kleure: harmonie in een toneel

worked_example.final_answer: Related colours, such as blues and greens.

practice_questions.correct_answer: Careful observation leads to a more convincing final image.

practice_questions.hint_af: Dink aan hoe goed jy iets kan teken wat jy nie noukeurig bekyk het nie.

practice_questions.correct_answer: Any reasonable example, e.g. a bright-coloured animal against a duller background.
practice_questions.hint_en: Think about light versus dark, or bright versus dull.
practice_questions.hint_af: Dink aan lig teenoor donker, of helder teenoor dof.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Create in 3D: wild or domestic animals

source_trace: Skills: earthenware clay. Art elements: texture, shape/form reinforced through modelling. Design principles: reinforce contrast and proportion. Spatial awareness: reinforce working in space.
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 51, Grade 4 Term 3 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Model a wild or domestic animal using earthenware clay.
Reinforce texture and shape/form to represent the animal convincingly.
Reinforce contrast, proportion, and spatial awareness (front, back, sides) in your model.

english_content.narration_script: This term you'll model a wild or domestic animal in earthenware clay, reinforcing skills you've already begun building this year. Texture is especially important for animals: think about how you'd represent fur, scales, or feathers differently in clay -- perhaps scratching fine lines for fur, or smoothing the surface for scales. Shape and form matter too: an animal's body has a distinct silhouette and structure that needs to read clearly even without colour. As before, reinforce contrast and proportion in your model -- getting the relative size of the head, body, and legs right (or stylising them deliberately) makes a real difference to how convincing your animal looks. And don't forget spatial awareness: your clay animal needs to be considered from the front, back, and both sides, since it exists in real space, not just from the one angle you might be most focused on while you work. Take a moment before you finish to walk around your model and check it from every side. Let's think through the deliberate-exaggeration question a bit further, since it connects directly to the visual literacy lesson you studied before starting this project. If you decide to stylise your animal rather than model it perfectly realistically -- giving it oversized eyes or an especially expressive pose -- that's a genuine artistic decision, not a mistake, as long as you make it on purpose rather than by accident. The key difference between a stylised choice and a simple error is whether you can explain why you made it: 'I made the eyes bigger to make my lizard look more alert and alive' is a real artistic reason, while 'I just couldn't get the proportions right' is not. As you finish your model this term, try to be able to explain every deliberate choice you made -- your texture choices, your proportions, your emphasis -- since being able to explain your own artistic decisions is just as valuable a skill as making them well in the first place. One final tip: keep a small bowl of water nearby while you work, since slightly dampening your fingers or tools makes fine texture marks -- scales, fur lines, feather layers -- much easier to control than working with completely dry clay, which tends to crack and crumble under detailed, repeated marking.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A clay animal model with texture tools scratching in fur-like lines, then the model being turned to show all sides.
visual_storyboard.on_screen_text: Texture, form, and all-round spatial awareness

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vanjaar sal jy 'n wilde of mak dier in erdewerk-klei modelleer, en vaardighede versterk wat jy reeds vanjaar begin bou het. Tekstuur is besonder belangrik vir diere: dink aan hoe jy pels, skubbe, of vere verskillend in klei sou voorstel -- miskien fyn lyne krap vir pels, of die oppervlak glad maak vir skubbe. Vorm is ook belangrik: 'n dier se liggaam het 'n duidelike silhoeët en struktuur wat duidelik moet lees selfs sonder kleur. Soos voorheen, versterk kontras en proporsie in jou model -- om die relatiewe grootte van die kop, liggaam, en pote reg te kry (of dit doelbewus te stileer) maak 'n regte verskil aan hoe oortuigend jou dier lyk. En moenie ruimtelike bewustheid vergeet nie: jou kleidier moet van voor, agter, en albei kante oorweeg word, aangesien dit in werklike ruimte bestaan, nie net vanuit die een hoek waarop jy dalk die meeste fokus terwyl jy werk nie. Neem 'n oomblik voor jy klaarmaak om om jou model te loop en dit van elke kant te kontroleer. Kom ons dink deur die doelbewuste-oordrywing-vraag 'n bietjie verder, aangesien dit direk verband hou met die visuele geletterdheid-les wat jy voor hierdie projek bestudeer het. As jy besluit om jou dier te stileer eerder as om dit perfek realisties te modelleer -- deur dit oorgrootte oë of 'n besonder uitdrukkingsvolle houding te gee -- is dit 'n ware kunssinnige besluit, nie 'n fout nie, solank jy dit doelbewus maak eerder as per ongeluk. Die sleutelverskil tussen 'n gestileerde keuse en 'n eenvoudige fout is of jy kan verduidelik hoekom jy dit gemaak het: 'ek het die oë groter gemaak om my akkedis meer wakker en lewendig te laat lyk' is 'n ware kunssinnige rede, terwyl 'ek kon net nie die proporsies reg kry nie' is nie. Terwyl jy jou model vanjaar afhandel, probeer om elke doelbewuste keuse wat jy gemaak het te kan verduidelik -- jou tekstuurkeuses, jou proporsies, jou klem -- aangesien om jou eie kunssinnige besluite te kan verduidelik net so waardevolle vaardigheid is as om hulle goed te maak in die eerste plek. Een finale wenk: hou 'n klein bak water byderhand terwyl jy werk, aangesien om jou vingers of gereedskap effens te bevogtig fyn tekstuurmerke -- skubbe, pelslyne, veerlae -- baie makliker maak om te beheer as om met heeltemal droë klei te werk, wat geneig is om te kraak en te verkrummel onder gedetailleerde, herhaalde merking.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: 'n Kleidiermodel met tekstuurgereedskap wat pels-agtige lyne inkrap, dan die model word gedraai om alle kante te wys.

worked_example.problem_af: Hoe sou jy wys dat 'n dier vere het, eerder as pels of skubbe, deur kleitekstuurtegnieke te gebruik?
solution_steps: Consider the different surface qualities of fur, scales, and feathers.
Feathers could be shown with layered, overlapping marks, different from fine fur lines or smooth scale patterns.
worked_example.final_answer: By using layered, overlapping texture marks distinct from fur's fine lines or scales' smooth pattern.

practice_questions.correct_answer: It helps represent fur, scales, or feathers convincingly.

practice_questions.correct_answer: That it looks considered and complete from the front, back, and sides.
practice_questions.hint_en: Think about spatial awareness.
practice_questions.hint_af: Dink aan ruimtelike bewustheid.

practice_questions.question_en: Why might you deliberately exaggerate an animal's proportions in your model?
practice_questions.question_af: Hoekom sou jy doelbewus 'n dier se proporsies in jou model oordryf?
practice_questions.correct_answer: To create a stylised rather than fully realistic effect.
practice_questions.hint_en: Think about cartoon-style animals.
practice_questions.hint_af: Dink aan spotprentstyl-diere.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Visual literacy: art elements found in the natural world

source_trace: Observe and discuss visual stimuli to identify art elements found in the natural world, and examples of contrast and proportion.
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 51, Grade 4 Term 4 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Identify art elements found in photographs and artworks of the natural world.
Identify examples of contrast and proportion in nature.
Apply this observation skill to your own nature-themed artwork.

english_content.narration_script: This term, we turn our visual literacy skills toward the natural world -- trees, leaves, flowers, rocks, clouds, water. Look at photographs and artworks of nature and identify the art elements present: shape (the outline of a leaf or mountain), texture (rough bark, smooth petals), and colour, which nature offers in extraordinary variety. Now look specifically for contrast and proportion. Contrast appears everywhere in nature -- a dark tree trunk against a bright sky, rough bark against smooth new leaves. Proportion shows up too: think about how a tiny flower relates in size to a huge tree, or how the branches of a tree relate in size to its trunk. Nature is actually one of the richest possible sources for studying art elements and design principles, since these same qualities -- contrast, proportion, texture -- exist all around us, long before any human artist ever picked up a pencil. Practising this kind of observation prepares you well for your own natural-world artwork this term. Let's push this observation a step further with a specific example: think about a photograph of a spider's web covered in morning dew. The web itself shows delicate, radiating lines; the dew drops show smooth, rounded shapes with tiny highlights of colour and light; and the contrast between the fine web and the solid leaves or branches behind it makes the whole scene visually striking. Nobody designed this scene -- it happened naturally, which is exactly the point: the same principles artists use deliberately in their work are simply built into how the natural world looks. This is worth remembering whenever you feel stuck for artistic ideas: stepping outside and looking closely at a leaf, a rock, or a spider's web will almost always reveal genuine examples of shape, texture, contrast, and proportion already arranged in ways worth learning from. For your own observation exercise this week, try photographing three completely different natural objects -- a leaf, a stone, and a cloud, for example -- and see how many of shape, texture, colour, contrast, and proportion you can identify in each one, comparing how differently these same qualities show up across such different subjects.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A nature photograph (tree against sky) with labels pointing to contrast (dark trunk/bright sky) and proportion (branch size versus trunk size).

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vanjaar draai ons ons visuele geletterdheid-vaardighede na die natuurlike wêreld -- bome, blare, blomme, rotse, wolke, water. Kyk na foto's en kunswerke van die natuur en identifiseer die kunselemente teenwoordig: vorm (die omtrek van 'n blaar of berg), tekstuur (growwe bas, gladde blomblare), en kleur, wat die natuur in buitengewone verskeidenheid bied. Kyk nou spesifiek vir kontras en proporsie. Kontras verskyn orals in die natuur -- 'n donker boomstam teen 'n helder lug, growwe bas teen gladde nuwe blare. Proporsie kom ook voor: dink aan hoe 'n piepklein blom in grootte met 'n enorme boom verband hou, of hoe die takke van 'n boom in grootte met sy stam verband hou. Die natuur is eintlik een van die rykste moontlike bronne om kunselemente en ontwerpbeginsels te bestudeer, aangesien hierdie selfde eienskappe -- kontras, proporsie, tekstuur -- reeds om ons bestaan, lank voordat enige menslike kunstenaar ooit 'n potlood opgetel het. Om hierdie soort waarneming te oefen berei jou goed voor vir jou eie natuurwêreld-kunswerk vanjaar. Kom ons stoot hierdie waarneming 'n stap verder met 'n spesifieke voorbeeld: dink aan 'n foto van 'n spinnekopweb bedek met oggenddou. Die web self wys delikate, stralende lyne; die douppels wys gladde, ronde vorms met piepklein hoogtepunte van kleur en lig; en die kontras tussen die fyn web en die soliede blare of takke daaragter maak die hele toneel visueel opvallend. Niemand het hierdie toneel ontwerp nie -- dit het natuurlik gebeur, wat presies die punt is: dieselfde beginsels wat kunstenaars doelbewus in hul werk gebruik is eenvoudig ingebou in hoe die natuurlike wêreld lyk. Dit is die moeite werd om te onthou wanneer jy ook al vasgevang voel vir kunssinnige idees: om buite te stap en noukeurig na 'n blaar, 'n rots, of 'n spinnekopweb te kyk sal amper altyd ware voorbeelde van vorm, tekstuur, kontras, en proporsie reeds gerangskik op maniere die moeite werd om van te leer, openbaar. Vir jou eie waarnemingsoefening hierdie week, probeer drie heeltemal verskillende natuurlike voorwerpe fotografeer -- 'n blaar, 'n klip, en 'n wolk, byvoorbeeld -- en kyk hoeveel van vorm, tekstuur, kleur, kontras, en proporsie jy in elkeen kan identifiseer, en vergelyk hoe verskillend hierdie selfde eienskappe oor sulke verskillende onderwerpe opduik.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: 'n Natuurfoto (boom teen lug) met etikette wat na kontras (donker stam/helder lug) en proporsie (takgrootte teenoor stamgrootte) wys.

worked_example.problem_af: Jy sien 'n foto van 'n klein voëltjie wat op 'n enorme boomtak sit. Watter ontwerpseienskap illustreer dit?
solution_steps: This is about a size relationship between the bird and the branch.
Size relationships are proportion.
worked_example.final_answer: Proportion.

practice_questions.question_en: Name one example of contrast you might see in nature.

practice_questions.correct_answer: Any reasonable example, e.g. dark tree trunk against a bright sky.
practice_questions.hint_en: Think about dark versus light, or rough versus smooth.
practice_questions.hint_af: Dink aan donker teenoor lig, of growwig teenoor glad.

practice_questions.question_en: Why might nature be a rich source for studying art elements?
practice_questions.question_af: Hoekom mag die natuur 'n ryk bron wees om kunselemente te bestudeer?
practice_questions.correct_answer: Because qualities like contrast, proportion and texture exist naturally all around us.
practice_questions.hint_en: Think about whether these qualities need a human artist to exist.
practice_questions.hint_af: Dink of hierdie eienskappe 'n menslike kunstenaar nodig het om te bestaan.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Create in 2D: the natural world

source_trace: Drawing and/or colour media exploring techniques. Art elements: reinforce secondary and related colour, including tints and shades. Design principles: reinforce contrast and proportion.
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 51, Grade 4 Term 4 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Create a 2D image of the natural world using a variety of media.
Reinforce secondary and related colour, and introduce tints and shades.
Reinforce contrast and proportion in your natural-world image.

english_content.narration_script: For your final drawing project this year, you'll create an image of the natural world -- a landscape, a plant, or a scene from nature. This term reinforces secondary and related colours you've already learned, and introduces something new: tints and shades. A tint is a colour mixed with white, making it lighter (like pink from red); a shade is a colour mixed with black, making it darker (like maroon from red). Using tints and shades lets you show light and shadow in nature far more convincingly -- the bright, tinted green of a sunlit leaf versus the darker, shaded green of one in shadow. As always, reinforce contrast and proportion: notice size relationships in your scene (a small flower against a large tree), and use clear visual differences to make parts of your image stand out. This project brings together everything you've explored in Visual Arts this year -- media exploration, colour theory, contrast, and proportion -- into one confident final piece. Let's work through the tint and shade idea with one more example, since it's genuinely useful across many future projects, not just this one. Imagine painting a red flower: mixing red with white gives you a lighter tint for the petals catching direct sunlight, while mixing red with black gives you a darker shade for the petals curled into shadow, and the pure, unmixed red itself can be used for the parts in between. Using all three -- the pure colour, a tint, and a shade -- rather than just one flat red, gives your flower a real sense of light falling across a three-dimensional form, rather than looking like a flat cutout. This same technique works for literally any colour and any subject, which is exactly why tints and shades are considered such a fundamental painting skill -- once you understand how to use them, you can make any flat colour feel like it has real light and shadow. Before you begin, it's worth sketching your composition lightly first, deciding roughly where your emphasis will fall and which colours will be tints versus shades, rather than discovering these choices only once you've already committed paint to the page -- a few minutes of planning here will save you from having to fight against an already-painted background later.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A single green colour being mixed with white to create a tint, and with black to create a shade, shown on a leaf illustration.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vir jou finale tekenprojek vanjaar sal jy 'n beeld van die natuurlike wêreld skep -- 'n landskap, 'n plant, of 'n toneel uit die natuur. Vanjaar versterk sekondêre en verwante kleure wat jy reeds geleer het, en stel iets nuuts bekend: tinte en skakerings. 'n Tint is 'n kleur gemeng met wit, wat dit ligter maak (soos pienk van rooi); 'n skakering is 'n kleur gemeng met swart, wat dit donkerder maak (soos maroen van rooi). Om tinte en skakerings te gebruik laat jou toe om lig en skaduwee in die natuur baie meer oortuigend te wys -- die helder, getinte groen van 'n sonverligte blaar teenoor die donkerder, geskakeerde groen van een in skaduwee. Soos altyd, versterk kontras en proporsie: let op groottewaarhoudinge in jou toneel ('n klein blom teen 'n groot boom), en gebruik duidelike visuele verskille om dele van jou beeld te laat uitstaan. Hierdie projek bring alles saam wat jy vanjaar in Visuele Kunste verken het -- media-verkenning, kleurteorie, kontras, en proporsie -- in een selfversekerde finale stuk. Kom ons werk die tint- en skakering-idee deur met nog 'n voorbeeld, aangesien dit werklik nuttig is oor baie toekomstige projekte, nie net hierdie een nie. Verbeel jou verf 'n rooi blom: om rooi met wit te meng gee jou 'n ligter tint vir die blomblare wat direkte sonlig vang, terwyl om rooi met swart te meng jou 'n donkerder skakering gee vir die blomblare wat in skaduwee opgekrul is, en die suiwer, ongemengde rooi self kan gebruik word vir die dele tussenin. Om al drie te gebruik -- die suiwer kleur, 'n tint, en 'n skakering -- eerder as net een plat rooi, gee jou blom 'n ware gevoel van lig wat oor 'n driedimensionele vorm val, eerder as om soos 'n plat uitknipsel te lyk. Hierdie selfde tegniek werk vir letterlik enige kleur en enige onderwerp, wat presies hoekom tinte en skakerings as so 'n fundamentele skildervaardigheid beskou word -- sodra jy verstaan hoe om hulle te gebruik, kan jy enige plat kleur laat voel asof dit werklike lig en skaduwee het. Voordat jy begin, is dit die moeite werd om jou komposisie eers liggies te skets, en ongeveer te besluit waar jou klem sal val en watter kleure tinte teenoor skakerings sal wees, eerder as om hierdie keuses eers te ontdek sodra jy reeds verf op die bladsy verbind het -- 'n paar minute se beplanning hier sal jou spaar om later teen 'n reeds-geverfde agtergrond te moet baklei.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Create in 3D: a kite, dream catcher, or bird feeder

source_trace: Recyclable materials. Skills: pasting, cutting, wrapping, tying, joining. Art elements: texture, shape/form, colour reinforced. Design principles: reinforce contrast and proportion. Spatial awareness:
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 51, Grade 4 Term 4 Visual Arts (detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Construct a kite, dream catcher, or bird feeder using recyclable materials and joining techniques.
Reinforce texture, shape/form, and colour in your construction.
Extend parts of your construction into space, showing advanced spatial awareness.

english_content.narration_script: For your final 3D project this year, choose one of three functional constructions: a kite, a dream catcher, or a bird feeder, built from recyclable materials like cardboard off-cuts, beads, sequins, ribbon, cotton, string, natural objects, and wood glue. This project reinforces skills you've built all year: pasting, cutting, wrapping, tying, and joining materials securely, and using texture, shape/form, and colour deliberately together. This term also pushes your spatial awareness further: rather than just making sure your object looks good from every side, try extending parts of your construction into space -- a dream catcher's hanging feathers, a kite's tail, or a bird feeder's perches all stick outward into three-dimensional space in ways a flat object never could. As always, reinforce contrast and proportion in your choices. Whichever object you choose, remember it should actually work as intended -- a kite should be shaped to catch wind, a bird feeder should be safe and functional for real birds -- combining genuine design thinking with your growing art skills. Let's think through the joining techniques question with a specific scenario: attaching a feather to a dream catcher's hoop securely enough that it will move gently in the wind without falling off. Tying works well here -- a length of cotton wrapped and knotted around both the feather's quill and the hoop holds firmly while still allowing movement, whereas pasting alone wouldn't hold up outdoors, and a rigid joint would stop the feather from moving naturally in the breeze, which is part of what makes a dream catcher feel alive. This is a good reminder that choosing a joining technique isn't just about what holds two things together most strongly -- it's about choosing the technique that suits how your finished object actually needs to behave. A kite needs joints that can flex under wind pressure without tearing; a bird feeder needs joints strong enough to hold weight safely; a dream catcher needs joints that allow gentle, natural movement. Thinking about your object's real function first will guide you toward the right technique every time. Whichever project you choose, build in a genuine testing step before calling it finished: actually fly your kite, hang your dream catcher where it will live, or check that your bird feeder can hold seed without spilling -- since real functional testing, not just a visual check, is what proves your design thinking actually worked.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: Three finished projects shown side by side: a colourful kite, a dream catcher with hanging feathers, and a simple bird feeder, each made from recyclable materials.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vir jou finale 3D-projek vanjaar, kies een van drie funksionele konstruksies: 'n vlieër, 'n droomvanger, of 'n voervoerder, gebou van herwinbare materiale soos kartonafsnitte, krale, flenters, lint, katoen, tou, natuurlike voorwerpe, en houtlym. Hierdie projek versterk vaardighede wat jy die hele jaar gebou het: plak, sny, toedraai, vasknoop, en materiale veilig aan mekaar verbind, en tekstuur, vorm, en kleur doelbewus saam gebruik. Vanjaar stoot ook jou ruimtelike bewustheid verder: eerder as om net seker te maak jou voorwerp lyk goed van elke kant, probeer dele van jou konstruksie in ruimte uitbrei -- 'n droomvanger se hangende vere, 'n vlieër se stert, of 'n voervoerder se sitplekke steek almal buitewaarts in driedimensionele ruimte uit op maniere wat 'n plat voorwerp nooit sou kon nie. Soos altyd, versterk kontras en proporsie in jou keuses. Watter voorwerp jy ook al kies, onthou dit behoort werklik te werk soos bedoel -- 'n vlieër moet gevorm word om wind te vang, 'n voervoerder moet veilig en funksioneel vir regte voëls wees -- wat werklike ontwerpdenke met jou groeiende kunsvaardighede kombineer. Kom ons dink deur die saamvoegtegniek-vraag met 'n spesifieke scenario: om 'n veer aan 'n droomvanger se hoepel veilig genoeg vas te maak sodat dit sag in die wind sal beweeg sonder om af te val. Vasknoop werk hier goed -- 'n lengte katoen om beide die veer se skag en die hoepel gedraai en geknoop hou ferm terwyl dit steeds beweging toelaat, terwyl plak alleen nie buite sou hou nie, en 'n stywe verbinding sou die veer keer om natuurlik in die wind te beweeg, wat deel is van wat 'n droomvanger laat lewend voel. Dit is 'n goeie herinnering dat om 'n saamvoegtegniek te kies nie net gaan oor wat twee dinge die sterkste saamhou nie -- dit gaan oor om die tegniek te kies wat pas by hoe jou voltooide voorwerp werklik moet gedra. 'n Vlieër het verbindings nodig wat onder windrukking kan buig sonder om te skeur; 'n voervoerder het verbindings nodig sterk genoeg om gewig veilig te hou; 'n droomvanger het verbindings nodig wat sagte, natuurlike beweging toelaat. Om eers oor jou voorwerp se werklike funksie te dink sal jou elke keer na die regte tegniek lei. Watter projek jy ook al kies, bou 'n ware toetsstap in voordat jy dit voltooid verklaar: vlieg werklik jou vlieër, hang jou droomvanger op waar dit sal woon, of kontroleer dat jou voervoerder saad kan hou sonder om te mors -- aangesien werklike funksionele toetsing, nie net 'n visuele kontrole nie, bewys jou ontwerpdenke het werklik gewerk.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Development of the self: self-concept, feedback, emotions, relationships

source_trace: Positive self-concept formation. Giving and receiving feedback. Coping with emotions: empathy, compassion, anger, disappointment, sadness. Relationships with peers, older people and strangers.
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 24, Grade 5 Term 1 (Personal and Social Well-being, detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Explain how others and personal successes influence positive self-concept formation.
Describe appropriate ways of giving and receiving both positive and negative feedback.
Distinguish between safe and unsafe relationships with peers, older people, and strangers.

english_content.narration_script: This term covers four connected ideas about growing as a person. First, positive self-concept: how you see and value yourself. This is influenced by others -- both adults and peers -- and by your own personal successes, which build confidence over time. It helps to have an action plan for continuing to build a positive self-concept, rather than leaving it to chance. Second, giving and receiving feedback: both from and to your peers and adults. There are appropriate ways to give feedback, whether positive or negative, focusing on the behaviour or work rather than attacking the person, and appropriate ways to receive feedback too, staying open rather than defensive. Third, coping with emotions: empathy, compassion, anger, disappointment, and sadness are all real, valid emotions, and this term focuses on skills to manage them in a positive way. Friends matter enormously here -- their significance in times of sadness, tragedy, and change cannot be overstated. Finally, relationships: with peers, older people, and strangers. Learning to tell the difference between safe and unsafe relationships, and good and bad ones, protects you, while understanding the real benefits of good, safe relationships helps you actively seek them out. Let's think through the safe-versus-unsafe relationship question a little further, since it's the most important idea in this whole lesson. A safe relationship, whether with a peer, an older person, or someone new, is generally one where you feel respected, where your boundaries are honoured, and where you feel comfortable saying no without fear of punishment or manipulation. An unsafe relationship often involves the opposite: pressure, secrecy, or a feeling that something isn't quite right, even if you can't always explain exactly why. Trusting that uneasy feeling, rather than dismissing it, is a genuinely important life skill. This connects directly to feedback too: a safe relationship usually allows for honest feedback given and received with care, while an unsafe one often punishes honesty or disagreement. As you think about your own relationships this term -- with friends, family, and people you're getting to know -- try to notice which of these signs, safe or unsafe, show up, and remember that a trusted adult is always a good person to talk to if something feels wrong.

visual_storyboard.visual_description: A learner building a wall of 'bricks' labelled with personal successes, forming a strong foundation labelled 'positive self-concept'.

A green checkmark over a 'safe relationship' scene (trusted adult, supportive friend) and a red cross over an 'unsafe relationship' warning scene.

afrikaans_content.narration_script: Vanjaar dek vier verbonde idees oor om as 'n persoon te groei. Eerste, positiewe selfbeeld: hoe jy jouself sien en waardeer. Dit word beïnvloed deur ander -- beide volwassenes en portuurgroep -- en deur jou eie persoonlike suksesse, wat mettertyd selfvertroue bou. Dit help om 'n aksieplan te hê om voort te gaan om 'n positiewe selfbeeld te bou, eerder as om dit aan die toeval oor te laat. Tweede, om terugvoer te gee en te ontvang: beide van en aan jou portuurgroep en volwassenes. Daar is toepaslike maniere om terugvoer te gee, of dit nou positief of negatief is, deur op die gedrag of werk te fokus eerder as om die persoon aan te val, en toepaslike maniere om terugvoer te ontvang ook, deur oop te bly eerder as verdedigend. Derde, om met emosies om te gaan: empatie, deernis, woede, teleurstelling, en hartseer is almal regte, geldige emosies, en vanjaar fokus op vaardighede om dit op 'n positiewe manier te bestuur. Vriende is hier enorm belangrik -- hul betekenis in tye van hartseer, tragedie, en verandering kan nie oorbeklemtoon word nie. Laastens, verhoudings: met portuurgroep, ouer mense, en vreemdelinge. Om die verskil tussen veilige en onveilige verhoudings, en goeie en slegte, te leer beskerm jou, terwyl om die werklike voordele van goeie, veilige verhoudings te verstaan jou help om hulle aktief te soek. Kom ons dink deur die veilige-teenoor-onveilige-verhouding-vraag 'n bietjie verder, aangesien dit die belangrikste idee in hierdie hele les is. 'n Veilige verhouding, of dit nou met 'n portuurgenoot, 'n ouer persoon, of iemand nuut is, is oor die algemeen een waar jy gerespekteer voel, waar jou grense geëer word, en waar jy gemaklik voel om nee te sê sonder vrees vir straf of manipulasie. 'n Onveilige verhouding behels dikwels die teenoorgestelde: druk, geheimhouding, of 'n gevoel dat iets nie heeltemal reg is nie, selfs al kan jy nie altyd presies verduidelik hoekom nie. Om daardie ongemaklike gevoel te vertrou, eerder as om dit af te maak, is 'n werklik belangrike lewensvaardigheid. Dit hou direk verband met terugvoer ook: 'n veilige verhouding laat gewoonlik eerlike terugvoer toe wat met sorg gegee en ontvang word, terwyl 'n onveilige een dikwels eerlikheid of meningsverskil straf. Terwyl jy vanjaar aan jou eie verhoudings dink -- met vriende, familie, en mense wat jy leer ken -- probeer opmerk watter van hierdie tekens, veilig of onveilig, opduik, en onthou 'n vertroude volwassene is altyd 'n goeie persoon om mee te praat as iets verkeerd voel.

subject: Life Skills
topic_name: Social responsibility: festivals and customs of religions in South Africa

source_trace: Festivals and customs from a variety of religions in South Africa.
lesson_metadata.source_section: Page 26, Grade 5 Term 3 (Personal and Social Well-being, detailed content, not the page overview table)

learning_objectives: Name a festival or custom from at least two different religions practised in South Africa.
Explain the meaning or purpose of one religious festival.
Show respect for religious practices different from your own.

english_content.narration_script: South Africa's many religions each celebrate their own festivals and customs, and learning about them helps us understand and respect the people around us. Think about festivals you might already know of: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights; Eid, celebrated by Muslims at the end of Ramadan; Christmas and Easter, celebrated by Christians; Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year; or Heritage-linked African religious ceremonies marking important life events. Each festival has its own meaning, often connected to a story, a historical event, or a spiritual belief, and its own customs -- special foods, clothing, decorations, or gatherings. Learning about these festivals isn't about deciding which is 'right' -- it's about building genuine respect and understanding for the diversity of belief in South Africa. When you meet a classmate or neighbour who celebrates a festival different from your own, that curiosity and respect helps build a stronger, more understanding community for everyone. Let's think a little more about how to respond if a classmate celebrates a festival you've never heard of, since that will genuinely happen. The best response is usually simple curiosity: asking a respectful question like 'what does that celebration mean to you?' or 'what do you do to celebrate?' shows genuine interest, rather than awkward silence or, worse, laughing at something unfamiliar. Notice too that many festivals, despite belonging to very different religions, actually share similar underlying purposes -- Diwali's lights and Christmas's lights both symbolise hope overcoming darkness, for instance, even though the specific stories behind them are completely different. Looking for these deeper connections, rather than only noticing surface differences like food or decorations, is exactly what turns simply knowing a list of festival names into genuinely understanding and respecting the people who celebrate them. As a small research task, ask a family member or neighbour who follows a religion different from your own about one festival they celebrate, and one custom connected to it -- a real conversation like this will almost always teach you something a textbook description alone never could. Bring what you learn back to class and share it -- your classmates will likely learn as much from your real conversation as you did.
